title: surface-review(examples-patterns): make Nine States managed loads newest-intent-wins
description:
## Slice reviewed

`examples/patterns/**`: boot, long-running work, nine states, and websocket, including their runnable build entries, adapter tests, governing pattern/spec text, and introducing history. This is the single cohesive correctness/teaching issue selected from that review.

## Correctness finding

The canonical Nine States example starts every data load with a direct `:rf.http/managed` effect but gives none of those requests a stable `:request-id`. That makes overlapping user intents first-settle-wins instead of newest-intent-wins.

The control panel leaves every Empty/One/Some/Too Many/error load button enabled whenever the page is not archived, including while the data region is already `:loading`. A second click therefore starts a second unkeyed request. The `:loading` state has no `:fetch-started` transition, so both requests remain in flight while the region stays at `:loading`. It accepts whichever `:fetch-succeeded` or `:fetch-failed` arrives first and immediately leaves `:loading`; its bucket/error states do not accept a completion. Thus an older request that was nearly finished can settle after a newer intent was issued, choose the visible bucket or error, and cause the newer request's eventual result to be ignored.

Concrete sequence: issue A for 25 rows, then issue B for 1 row before A settles. If A completes first, the page lands at `:too-many`; B later completes into a state that has no `:fetch-succeeded` handler, so the requested `:one` result never appears. The same ownership hole crosses success/failure: a nearly-complete old failing request can put the page in `:error` while a newer success is still in flight, then discard that success.

This is exactly the stale-reply case the governing pattern calls out. `spec/Pattern-NineStates.md` says a fresh load must prevent the previous reply from landing and demonstrates a stable `:request-id`; managed HTTP already gives the minimal mechanism: issuing the same id supersedes the old attempt and suppresses its app reply. The example omitted that one field.

## Evidence

- `examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs:463-488`: both `:nine-states.demo/load` and `:nine-states.demo/load-with-failure` broadcast `:fetch-started` and issue `:rf.http/managed`; neither args map has `:request-id`.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs:490-502`: every success/failure callback is forwarded unconditionally as a machine completion, with no ownership token or stale check.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs:339-385`: only `:loading` consumes `:fetch-succeeded` / `:fetch-failed`; `:loading` itself does not consume another `:fetch-started`, and the settled bucket/error states consume only a future `:fetch-started` or reset. This makes the first completion decisive.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs:756-782`: load controls are disabled only by `:mode/read-only`, not by `:data/loading`, so overlap is a supported interaction, not merely a fabricated internal event.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/stories.cljs:116-159`: the Story twins reproduce the same managed-request envelopes without a request id. Their canned fxs are synchronous, so the omission is visually hidden there too.
- `spec/Pattern-NineStates.md:289-313`: the canonical direct-managed-HTTP handler includes `:request-id :counter/load`.
- `spec/Pattern-NineStates.md:342-359`: direct effects do not get actor-lifetime cancellation; the stale-detection section says a fresh load while a previous request is live must not admit the previous reply, and names stable same-id supersession as the common-case mechanism.
- `docs/async/http.md:24-37`: public managed-HTTP reference defines `:request-id` as the stable id whose reuse supersedes the old request.
- `implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_cljs_test.cljs:1503-1547`: the CLJS transport regression proves same-id supersession delivers no app reply from the superseded request.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/nine_states_cljs_test.cljs:80-132`: the example suite routes HTTP to the synchronous demo stub; it even has to manufacture `:loading` by dispatching `:fetch-started` alone. These one-at-a-time rows cannot exercise overlap.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/nine_states_cljs_test.cljs:260-283`: the only stale-completion test resets to `:nothing` and sends a completion while still at `:nothing`, where it is trivially ignored. It does not exercise reset-then-reload or two live attempts, where the region is back at `:loading` and will accept the old completion.

## History

`1392aa0d1e` (2026-05-11) introduced the current load handlers without request ids. `git log -S":request-id" -- examples/patterns/nine_states/core.cljs` returns no commit: this path has never owned one. Sixteen minutes after the example rewrite, `a385d1aaba` added the managed-HTTP integration to `Pattern-NineStates`, including the stable request id and the explicit stale/supersession rationale. Later edits improved replies, schemas, reset semantics, frames, and prose, but never reconciled this executable companion with that requirement.

## Bounded recommendation

Define one clearly named stable request id for the Nine States data-load lane and put it on both live request shapes (`load` and `load-with-failure`), so any newer load intent supersedes either kind of older attempt. Carry the same field in the Story twins so the teaching envelopes remain faithful even though canned stubs do not model a real in-flight registry. Add a short adjacent explanation: the id expresses ownership of one replaceable page-load slot; it is not incidental tracing metadata.

Add one deterministic single-frame CLJS composition regression with a controlled/deferred transport: issue A, issue B before A settles, prove A's app target is suppressed, then settle B and prove only B's exact items/failure choose the machine state. Include a cross-kind row or table case so `load` and `load-with-failure` cannot accidentally drift onto separate ids.

This is the pre-alpha ergonomic fix: one existing field, one shared constant, one behavioral witness. It trusts the programmer and keeps all concurrency policy in readable data instead of disabling buttons or building a coordinator abstraction.

## Non-goals

- Do not redesign the parallel machine, cardinality cascade, render-priority table, or reply handlers.
- Do not add a request manager, sequence counter, promise layer, or generic remote-data abstraction.
- Do not disable load controls while loading; that only hides the race from mouse users and leaves programmatic intents incorrect.
- Do not move this example to the `:rf.http/managed` machine wrapper solely for this fix.
- Do not add a connection/page epoch to this non-routed, single-frame demo unless a separate lifecycle case proves it necessary. Stable same-id supersession closes the demonstrated overlap and reset-then-reload window.
- Do not change managed HTTP, canned-stub semantics, or the other three pattern examples.

## Duplicate search

Immediately before creation I searched all statuses in `.beads/issues.jsonl` with targeted `rg` combinations for Nine States/nine_states plus `request-id`, `stale`, `supersession`, `first-settle`, `newest`, `overlap`, and `demo/load`. No issue owns this example-level omission.

Closest open issue `rf2-o8ek` concerns the HTTP implementation's process-global registry colliding when two different frames reuse the same raw request id. It is complementary, not duplicate: this bead is a single-frame caller that supplies no id at all, so it cannot get supersession even after `rf2-o8ek` lands. The proposed regression is intentionally single-frame. Closed `rf2-iyjae` concerns websocket inbound correlation/validation, a different example and transport boundary.

## Uncertainty

Per review dispatch, I did not run a browser/runtime or external network. The verdict is derived from the executable transition tables, request envelopes, synchronous-test setup, current managed-HTTP contract, and its existing CLJS supersession regression. The exact controlled-fetch helper can follow the HTTP suite's established harness rather than inventing a new one. The canned demo resolves synchronously, so the current clickable app may not visibly reproduce the race until its override is replaced by the real asynchronous transport—the exact copy/adaptation moment this canonical example is meant to guide.
design: Use one stable keyword/constant for the replaceable Nine States data-load slot and attach it to every request producer in this example. Keep stale arbitration in the existing managed-HTTP boundary: same-id issue supersedes the previous attempt and the old app reply is suppressed before the page handler can broadcast it into the machine. Do not add local sequence bookkeeping. Test through a real controlled managed-HTTP lifecycle in one frame, because the canned effect intentionally has no in-flight lifecycle and cannot prove supersession.
acceptance_criteria:
- `:nine-states.demo/load` and `:nine-states.demo/load-with-failure` issue `:rf.http/managed` with the same stable, namespaced request id; the two Story request twins carry that same ownership field for envelope fidelity.
- A deterministic CLJS test in one frame holds request A open, issues request B through the shipped example event before A settles, and proves A's later success or failure dispatch reaches no app target and cannot move or mutate the Nine States machine.
- Settling B produces exactly B's expected `:items`/`:error`, data-region state/tag, and `:ui/render` result. At least one table row crosses request kind (old success versus new failure, or old failure versus new success) so both producer events are proven to share one replacement lane.
- A reset-then-new-load sequence cannot be overwritten by the pre-reset attempt; either cover it directly or make the overlap test's same-id suppression mechanism and existing reset test jointly explicit.
- The regression uses the real managed-HTTP supersession path or an existing controlled transport seam, not only the synchronous canned stub and not a hand-dispatched `:fetch-succeeded` event. A negative control removing/changing the shared request id makes the new overlap witness fail.
- Existing nine-state, reset, Story lifecycle, example compile/asset, and relevant managed-HTTP CLJS tests remain green. Reader-facing prose near the request explains newest-intent ownership in a few lines without adding a new abstraction.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #9242 (branch worker/expat-a), entirely inside examples/patterns/**.

ESTABLISHED AT SOURCE, the three questions the fix turned on:
(a) How the example keys request-ids: it did not. Neither :nine-states.demo/load nor :nine-states.demo/load-with-failure carried :request-id, and re_frame/http/registry.cljc states it outright — 'An anonymous request (no :request-id) never supersedes'. So no supersession was reachable.
(b) Whether a newer intent re-issues: yes. Every load button dispatches the load event again, which issues a fresh :rf.http/managed. So supersession fires the moment an id exists — no correlation gate is needed on top.
(c) What the framework already does: everything required. handlers.cljc calls registry/supersede! on issue, which aborts the prior in-flight attempt under the same (frame, request-id) with :reason :request-id-superseded and suppresses its app reply before any handler sees it. #9202/#9212 (6aaddf52e3, 5c01850a80, 888833889b) made this frame-scoped without changing the criterion, so a plain reusable constant is safe.

CALL: adopt framework supersession, do NOT add a correlation gate. An example that hand-rolls a guard the framework provides teaches the wrong pattern, and spec/014 §791 names :request-id as THE app-level mechanism for requests dispatched directly from an event handler (which get no actor-destroy cascade). The :spawn/machine-wrapper route was also rejected on the merits, not merely by the non-goals: :loading has no :fetch-started self-transition, so a second load causes no region exit, hence no actor destroy, hence no abort — reaching that route would require reshaping the machine.

SHIPPED: one named constant, data-load-request-id (:nine-states.data/load), on both live request shapes and both Story twins; the twins reference the core var rather than copying the keyword (verified in the compiled artefact: nine_states.stories.js emits nine_states.core.data_load_request_id twice). Prose explains the id as ownership rather than tracing metadata, and records honestly that the demo :fx-overrides stub REPLACES :rf.http/managed outright, so the registry and supersession only run once a reader swaps in the real transport.

title: bug(machines-viz): SCXML import turns executable-content elements into fake states
description:
## Scope

Correct only the `tools/machines-viz` SCXML import boundary so non-state SCXML children cannot become re-frame2 `:states` entries and `scxml->spec` never returns a structurally invalid machine definition. Preserve the public `spec->scxml` / `scxml->spec` signatures, the supported topology mapping, the existing regex-reader posture, the id codec, and exporter round-trips.

## Correctness finding

`scxml->spec` silently turns ordinary SCXML executable-content elements into fake machine states. `group-children-by-state` says it pairs only `<state>` / `<final>` blocks, but after special-casing `<transition>` its `:self` and `:start` branches accept every tag. `consume-transitions` leaves non-transition elements such as `<onentry>`, `<onexit>`, `<datamodel>`, `<data>`, `<invoke>`, and `<log>` in `:children-tokens`; `parse-state-block` then feeds them to that broad grouper and maps every resulting block through `parse-state-block`. An element with no `id` becomes a state keyed by `nil` (`id-string->abs-path nil` -> `[nil]` -> local key `nil`). Multiple such elements can also overwrite one another in the resulting map.

The import path has no final canonical grammar check. `spec->scxml` validates with `grammar/valid-definition?` at `scxml.cljc:840-863`, and share/AI/Mermaid use the same projectability boundary, but `scxml->spec` returns its assembled map directly at lines 1462-1602. Thus the public importer can report success with a definition that `reg-machine`, `MachineChart`, every sibling emitter, and `grammar/valid-definition?` reject.

## Reproduction

A conforming SCXML 1.0 state may contain `<onentry>`; an empty `<onentry/>` is enough:

```clojure
(def xml
  "<scxml xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml' version='1.0' initial='idle'><state id='idle'><onentry/></state></scxml>")
(let [spec (scxml/scxml->spec xml)]
  {:spec spec
   :valid? (grammar/valid-definition? spec)
   :defect (grammar/definition-defect spec)})
```

Measured on current HEAD:

```clojure
{:spec {:states {:idle {:states {nil {}}}}, :initial :idle},
 :valid? false,
 :defect {:category :rf.error/machine-compound-state-missing-initial,
          :path [:idle]}}
```

A second measured case with `<onentry><log .../></onentry>` and a real `:go -> :done` transition preserved the transition but returned nested `{nil {:states {nil {}}}}`, proving this is not merely an empty-document edge.

W3C SCXML 1.0 section 3.3 explicitly permits `<onentry>` under `<state>`; the importer advertises interchange with external SCXML tooling and says unsupported executable bodies are lossy. Lossy/ignored is coherent. Inventing an occupiable nil-id state and returning an unusable definition is not.

## Evidence

- `tools/machines-viz/src/day8/re_frame2_machines_viz/scxml.cljc:1253-1314`: the child grouper's contract names `<state>` / `<final>`, but all non-transition `:self` / `:start` tokens are collected.
- `scxml.cljc:1137-1248`: only direct `<transition>` tokens are consumed/removed; other SCXML child elements remain for the broad grouper.
- `scxml.cljc:1340-1391`: `parse-state-block` derives every block's key from optional `id`, recursively treats grouped blocks as child states, and never checks the tag.
- `scxml.cljc:1462-1602`: `scxml->spec` checks non-string, missing root, unclosed containers, and empty top-level states, but never validates the returned definition.
- The public docstring at lines 1473-1478 says missing required structure throws `:scxml/invalid-spec`; returning invalid structure contradicts that error boundary.
- `tools/machines-viz/spec/API.md:2200-2231,2343-2354` presents `scxml->spec` as the inverse import and the canonical recursive grammar gate as the invalid-spec boundary.
- `tools/machines-viz/test/day8/re_frame2_machines_viz/scxml_cljs_test.cljc` heavily covers emitter-owned round-trips plus non-string/missing-root failures, but contains no `<onentry>`, `<onexit>`, `<datamodel>`, `<invoke>`, or unknown-element import case; emitter output never creates the triggering tokens.
- W3C authority: https://www.w3.org/TR/scxml/#state — `<onentry>` and `<onexit>` are valid `<state>` children.
- History: `git blame` attributes the broad grouper and return shape to the initial SCXML implementation, commit `1403ca5a69e` (2026-05-21). Later grammar and SCXML fixes hardened export, ids, action comments, history, and root-parallel transitions, but no history entry filters imported state children or validates the completed import.

## Impact

A programmer importing a normal external SCXML document can receive a plausible-looking EDN map that is unusable by the library. Failure is displaced to later registration/render/export, where it reports a misleading compound-state error about a state the programmer never authored. This defeats the ergonomic value of the interop seam and is especially hostile to AI/tooling pipelines, which reasonably trust `scxml->spec` success as its postcondition.

## Recommended bounded repair

1. Make the direct-child block collector classify only the tags the re-frame2 importer actually models (`state`, `final`, and `history`). Skip an unsupported self-closing element, and skip an unsupported open element together with its whole subtree so nested markup cannot be promoted accidentally. Continue handling direct transitions through the existing transition consumer.
2. Before returning from `scxml->spec`, validate the assembled definition with the existing `grammar/valid-definition?`. If parser output is not projectable, throw the documented `:scxml/invalid-spec` through the existing error builder with a value-free `grammar/definition-summary`; never return malformed data and never include the raw XML.
3. State the narrow import behavior in API/docs: unsupported executable/datamodel/invoke content is ignored/lossy; it is not reinterpreted as topology.

This is one tag allowlist at the existing collection boundary plus one shared postcondition check, not a new XML framework.

## Posture fit

This removes surprising behavior at a public conversion seam and reuses machinery already present. SPA programmers and agents get a simple law: successful import yields a machine the rest of re-frame2 accepts. No new public options, compatibility modes, AST, schema system, or abstraction is needed.

## Non-goals

- No execution or round-trip support for SCXML `<onentry>`, `<onexit>`, `<script>`, `<assign>`, `<log>`, `<datamodel>`, `<invoke>`, or other executable/data-model constructs.
- No replacement of the deliberately small regex reader with a full XML/SCXML processor.
- No expansion to XState JSON/Stately formats, nested-parallel semantics, or arbitrary namespace handling.
- No W3C omitted-`initial` defaulting or `<initial>`-element implementation in this task; preserve the currently documented requirement/rejection rather than broadening this repair.
- No change to export syntax, id encoding, action-comment lifting, or supported round-trip equality.

## Related / duplicate search

Tracked `.beads/issues.jsonl` searches for `SCXML default initial`, `SCXML first child`, `SCXML <initial>`, `group-children-by-state`, `fake/bogus nil state`, `non-state child`, `unknown XML element`, `SCXML onentry`, and `SCXML datamodel` found no relevant bead; no current issue title contains `SCXML`. Closed `rf2-sxw06` is the distinct one-click Mermaid workflow and closed `rf2-x19xi` is stale ELK arbitration. Historical SCXML commits (`rf2-mnp93.*`, `rf2-qgtcvy`, `rf2-j538f7.18`) address id/action/export/grammar issues, not this import classification.

## Uncertainty

The parser explicitly promises best-effort behavior for unsupported XML, so either ignore or a controlled parse error could be defensible for some foreign tags. The hard invariant is not ambiguous: success must never invent topology or return a definition the canonical grammar rejects. Ignoring standard executable/data-model children best matches the existing lossy contract and preserves useful topology import.

- A fixture with `<onentry><log/></onentry>`, `<onexit>`, `<datamodel><data/></datamodel>`, and `<invoke>` around otherwise supported states/transitions proves each unsupported subtree is ignored wholesale while the real state ids and transitions remain exact.
- An unsupported element containing a nested `<state>` does not promote that nested element into the parent's re-frame2 `:states`; only direct recognized state/history children are collected.
- Every successful `scxml->spec` result passes the canonical recursive grammar gate. Parser output that cannot be represented as a valid re-frame2 definition throws `:scxml/invalid-spec` with a value-free definition summary and no raw XML/content.
- Existing flat/compound/parallel/history/action/reenter/id-codec round-trips remain byte/value-equivalent, and malformed-root/unclosed-input error ids remain unchanged.
- Negative control: restoring the current catch-all self/start branches makes the new onentry fixture produce a nil-key state and fail the validity assertion.
- API/ns prose accurately describes unsupported SCXML child content as lossy/ignored and does not imply executable semantics were added.

title: epoch: lowering :depth leaves stale epochs queryable and restorable
description:
## Finding

Changing the live epoch `:depth` only updates the config atom; it does not resize the rings that already exist. The sharp case is `:depth 0`: because `record!` skips `append-record` entirely when depth is zero, retained records survive indefinitely. The public read and time-travel surfaces still consume them, so the documented “disabled ring” remains queryable and writable-through.

This is one configuration-transition defect, not a request for a new history abstraction.

## Verified reproduction

Reproduced at `52b2579e9b53816abddd3406f72db5a5278bed1c` on the JVM through the public API with the plain-atom adapter:

1. Make `:probe/frame`; dispatch `:probe/seed` to `{:n 1}` and `:probe/inc` to `{:n 2}`; save the first epoch id.
2. Before disabling, `(count (rf/epoch-history :probe/frame))` is `2` and app-db is `{:n 2}`.
3. Call `(rf/configure! {:epoch-history {:depth 0}})`.
4. Observed `(count (rf/epoch-history :probe/frame)) => 2`, then `(rf/restore-epoch! :probe/frame saved-id) => true`, and app-db rewound to `{:n 1}`. The probe exited 0.

A smaller data-level probe also recorded one row with `state/record!`, set depth to zero through `epoch/configure!`, and observed the same row from `epoch/epoch-history` afterwards.

Expected from the shipped contract: `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:118-123` says `epoch-history` is empty when depth is 0; its `configure!` doc at lines 57-63 says depth 0 disables recording and nothing lands in the ring. `spec/Tool-Pair.md:718` is explicit that setting depth 0 disables the per-frame ring and `epoch-history` returns `[]`, while listeners continue firing. The bounded-history rule at `spec/Tool-Pair.md:100` says the runtime keeps the last N epochs; lowering N should therefore make the live ring obey N, not wait for an unrelated future append.

## Cause and impact

- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch/state.cljc:55-83` (`merge-config!`) validates and swaps only `config`.
- `state.cljc:192-203` (`record!`) enforces the depth cap only on a later append, and its `(when (pos? history-depth) ...)` means depth 0 never reaches the cap logic.
- `state.cljc:205-208` (`history-for`) returns the retained vector without consulting the current depth.
- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch/tool_pair.cljc:409-410` and `:586-587` resolve restore/replay targets from that stale vector; `:2079-2081` projects it off-box.

Consequences are user-visible in the dev/tooling tier: the memory/retention knob does not release already-retained full frame-state and raw trace snapshots; an operator choosing “no retained history, listeners only” can still read/project old records; and old ids remain valid restore/replay inputs. Positive reductions have the same delayed behavior (the ring can exceed the new N until another record appends); zero is permanent because no append occurs to repair it.

## Bounded recommendation

Make a valid `:depth` reduction enforce the new cap against every existing per-frame ring at the configuration boundary. Preserve newest-first retention semantics: depth N keeps each frame’s newest N existing records; depth 0 drops them all. Reconcile any internal last-settled/back-fill anchors that would otherwise keep naming removed records, so disabling then re-enabling starts from a genuinely empty history rather than resurrecting or targeting an old epoch. Keep the existing depth-0 listener contract: newly assembled records still fan out raw to registered epoch listeners but are not retained.

Prefer the smallest change around `re-frame.epoch.state/merge-config!` and its storage helpers. The implementation may choose its own synchronization shape; the observable invariant is that once `configure!` returns, every ring respects the accepted depth.

## Posture rationale

This closes a broken existing knob and removes surprise from a core SPA debugging gesture. It gives people and AI tools one honest meaning for “history depth” without adding API, modes, compatibility branches, or policy. The value is correctness and low-friction ergonomics, not a more elaborate timeline system.

## Non-goals

- No branching timeline, archive/export, persistence, or new clear-history API.
- No change to listener publication at depth 0.
- No new error category and no change to normal restore/replay semantics for records that remain retained.
- No retroactive rewrite of record payloads or `:trace-events-keep` semantics beyond what is necessary to keep the accepted depth invariant.
- No unrelated cleanup of the epoch state atoms or concurrency machinery.

## Duplicate and history search

All-status bead searches were run for epoch titles and description phrases `depth 0`, `ring disabled`, `disables recording`, `lowering depth`, `stale history`, `epoch-history returns`, `epoch-history`, `trace-events-keep`, and `history-for`. No bead describes this config-transition defect. The two all-status `depth 0` description hits were unrelated: `rf2-5mr6` (malformed routing fixture) and `rf2-6ka0` (retired tools-root prose). Relevant closed work is adjacent but distinct: `rf2-gba3ou` covers leakage of the `replace-history-disabled` trace; commits `417628bdd9` / `4aec0cbfc5` reject state injection at depth 0 and pin back-fill snapshot consistency. Neither trims a pre-existing ring on configuration change.

Path history and `git blame` show `merge-config!` / `history-for` originated in the epoch cohesion split (`cd9fdb75587`); later naming and depth-0 work did not add a transition-time trim. `git log --all --grep=depth.0` and retention searches found no commit claiming this behavior.

## Uncertainties

The contract is clear for the post-return observable state, but the best internal synchronization with a JVM append racing `configure!` needs implementation-time judgment. A focused test should pin the synchronous public behavior first; add a race test only if the chosen implementation introduces a meaningful interleaving, rather than building machinery speculatively.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A public-API test records several epochs in at least two frames, lowers `:depth` to a positive N, and immediately (without another dispatch) sees only each frame’s newest N records.
2. A public-API test records an epoch, sets `:depth 0`, and immediately sees `[]` from both `rf/epoch-history` and `rf/projected-history`; the saved id can no longer be restored or replayed and frame state is unchanged by those refusals.
3. Depth 0 continues to publish newly assembled records to epoch listeners while retaining none.
4. Re-enabling a positive depth after the zero-depth interval starts with no pre-disable records; a new dispatch records normally, and post-settle back-fill cannot target a retired epoch id.
5. Existing invalid-config, ring-eviction, restore/replay, listener, and production-elision tests remain green. Add focused coverage in `implementation/epoch/test/re_frame/epoch_test.clj` and the representative CLJS epoch suite for the cross-platform public behavior.
6. No public API, error vocabulary, or compatibility alias is added.

title: surface-review(uix-adapter): imperative effect retains the old frame dispatcher after provider swaps
description:
## Scope

Correct the canonical UIx imperative-lifecycle recipe so a listener installed by `uix/use-effect` follows the frame selected by `re-frame.adapter.uix/use-frame`. This is the public copy/paste path for DOM listeners and third-party widgets, not a request to expand the adapter API.

## Verified behavior

`implementation/adapters/uix/README.md:56-66` currently does this in `tile-inner`:

```clojure
(let [ref (uix/use-ref)
      {:keys [dispatch]} (uix-adapter/use-frame)]
  (uix/use-effect
    (fn []
      (let [listener (fn [_evt]
                       (dispatch [:tile/finished-merging tile-id]))]
        (.addEventListener (.-current ref) "animationend" listener)
        (fn [] (.removeEventListener (.-current ref) "animationend" listener))))
    [tile-id]))
```

The effect closes over TWO reactive render values, `tile-id` and `dispatch`, but its dependency vector names only `tile-id`. The same README immediately says at `:79` to include every value the effect reads.

This omission is routing-significant, not merely lint style:

1. `implementation/core/src/re_frame/adapter/use_frame.cljs:99-128` consumes the shared React context and memoizes the capture bundle only for one resolved frame incarnation. A provider change re-renders the component and returns a new ops map/new `dispatch`; the public contract says so at `implementation/adapters/uix/src/re_frame/adapter/uix.cljs:160-168` and `docs/api/re-frame.adapter.uix.md:120-122`.
2. UIx 1.4.4's published source (`uix/core.clj`, `make-hook-with-deps`; `uix/hooks/alpha.cljs`, `use-clj-deps` + `use-effect`) sends the declared vector to React and only changes that dependency array when the CLJS vector is unequal. Function equality is identity, so adding `dispatch` does exactly what this API designed its reference stability to support: no rerun for the same frame, rerun for a changed frame bundle. UIx's official hook docs confirm the vector/dependency comparison: https://github.com/pitch-io/uix/blob/master/docs/hooks.md#dependency-array . Its exhaustive-deps linter also reports component-body free variables omitted from the vector (`uix/linter.clj`, `lint-exhaustive-deps!` / `::missing-deps`).
3. React runs effect cleanup/setup again only when a declared dependency changes and requires every reactive value used by setup to be listed: https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect#parameters .

Therefore, with frame A and frame B both live, rerendering the same mounted `tile-inner` beneath a provider changed from A to B while `tile-id` is unchanged yields a fresh B-locked `dispatch` in the render, but DOES NOT replace the installed listener. `animationend` still invokes the closure installed under A and silently dispatches `:tile/finished-merging` into A. If A was destroyed instead, the stale capture fence drops the event and emits the destroyed-frame error. Either result contradicts the recipe's promise to carry “the surrounding frame” and the hook's provider-retarget contract.

## Existing coverage and the gap

- `implementation/adapters/uix/test/re_frame/adapter/uix_use_subscribe_dom_cljs_test.cljs:465-476` forwards the shared `use-frame` shape/stability/reincarnation assertions.
- `implementation/core/test/re_frame/adapter/react_shared_suite.cljs:3904-3978` proves the bundle is stable for the same frame and that an extracted op dispatches after render.
- `implementation/core/test/re_frame/adapter/react_shared_suite.cljs:3980-4079` proves a forced next render after same-id reincarnation returns a new bundle and the old bundle is inert.
- No adapter test composes `use-frame` with a long-lived `use-effect`/DOM listener while the provider target changes. The README snippet is not compiled by the existing docs-pin test (`uix_component_recipe_docs_pin_test.clj` pins the separate component-testing recipe), so UIx's exhaustive-deps warning and the stale listener both escape CI.

## Bounded recommendation

- Change the canonical effect deps to `[tile-id dispatch]` and make the adjacent sentence say that the deps include every reactive value captured by the effect, explicitly including frame-bound callbacks from `use-frame`.
- Add one focused UIx browser regression, near `uix_use_subscribe_dom_cljs_test.cljs` or in a small dedicated `*_dom_cljs_test.cljs`: create live frames A and B with distinguishable handlers/state; mount one listener-bearing `defui` under `frame-provider` A; rerender the same component/key under provider B without changing its domain prop; fire the DOM event; assert B alone changes. Also assert the old listener was cleaned up (one event => one dispatch) and unmount in `finally`.
- Compile the real recipe shape in that test so UIx's own exhaustive-deps analysis guards the dependency list. Keep the browser-lane test narrow; no general Markdown-snippet compiler is needed.

## Impact

This is a cross-frame correctness failure in the exact escape hatch recommended for maps, editors, charts, animation callbacks, browser APIs, and third-party stores. A tenant/tab/provider switch can mutate the previously selected live frame while the UI shows the new one—a silent isolation failure. The minimal dependency fix uses the stability guarantee `use-frame` already provides and imposes no effect churn within one frame.

## Posture rationale

Pre-alpha is the right time to make the one canonical SPA recipe exact. One dependency plus one behavioral pin is high leverage: it preserves a tiny API, trusts normal React/UIx dependency semantics, and prevents a class of wrong-frame writes without inventing an event wrapper, effect-event helper, provider generation counter, or adapter machinery.

## Non-goals

- No new public API or hook, and no change to `use-frame`, `capture-frame`, provider, or frame lifecycle semantics.
- No generalized hook linter/doc-snippet framework and no audit of every effect in the repository.
- No requirement to remount providers/components on frame changes; provider retargeting is already a supported contract.
- Do not fold the separate README claim about bare no-arg `capture-frame` context resolution into this fix; it is independent of the stale-effect dependency.

## Duplicate search

Searched all 922 beads (open/deferred/closed) by title/description/notes and repository history before filing. Description searches for `tile-inner`, `finished-merging`, `stale dispatch`, `dispatch dependency`, `use-effect`, `effect deps`, `provider swap`, `stale closure`, and `imperative escape` each returned zero. Broader `UIx`/`use-frame` results were reviewed; the closest are closed `rf2-9hcyf` (copy-complete UIx component *testing*, a different recipe), `rf2-yrq9n` (adapter wording/retired Helix), and `rf2-oz7wr` (registered-view head cache). Commit history shows the affected snippet arrived in `4d24ca4376`, switched to `use-frame` in `f013dd2807`, and has retained `[tile-id]`; `bbdcc8ba53` explicitly introduced the provider-swap/reference-stability guarantee that makes `dispatch` a cheap and necessary dependency. No tracked or already-fixed issue matches this behavior.

## Uncertainties

I did not execute the browser lane in this review worktree because it intentionally has no `node_modules` link and the review brief prohibited creating one. The failure is derived from the checked-in adapter implementation, the exact published UIx 1.4.4 sources already in the dependency cache, the official UIx/React hook contracts, and the uncompiled README code. The focused acceptance test should be the final executable proof and should use a live A -> live B provider swap; a destroy/recreate-only test would exercise the stale-frame fence but miss the more serious silent write into still-live A.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The UIx README's `tile-inner` effect declares both captured reactive values, `[tile-id dispatch]`, and adjacent guidance explicitly includes frame-bound callbacks returned by `use-frame`.
2. A real-browser UIx test mounts a listener-bearing component under live frame A, rerenders the same component/key under live frame B with its domain prop unchanged, fires the event, and proves B changes while A does not.
3. The test proves effect cleanup/reinstall is balanced (one event produces one dispatch), guarantees unmount/runtime cleanup, and exercises the actual `uix/use-effect` + `uix-adapter/use-frame` spelling.
4. The UIx browser test lane and relevant docs/link gates pass. No public API or runtime adapter machinery is added.
notes: Surface-review partition: implementation/adapters/uix/**. Reviewed adapter source, README/public API/spec contract, all adapter test entry points and the shared React suite they forward, standalone testbed and real UIx examples, published UIx 1.4.4 source, official React/UIx hook docs, existing beads, and relevant history. Worker guard passed immediately before creation with WORKTREE_ROOT=C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2-worktrees\codex-reviewpool-d, BRANCH=worker/codex-reviewpool-d.
close_reason:
MERGED as PR #9264 (mayor fast-forwarded to dc795fb3b5; five clauses met — see rf2-f8wu's close reason for the clause-5 note about the raw workflow line count reading 40 while job keys read 0).

PREMISE HELD AT SOURCE and the bead was unchanged since creation (single updated_at), so its description governed — unlike its sibling on this PR. The UIx README's imperative-effect example declared deps [tile-id] and omitted the dispatcher, so after a provider swap the effect kept dispatching into the OLD frame. Frames are isolated contexts in this project, so that is an isolation break rather than staleness. Fixed to [tile-id dispatch], with the two prose claims that made the omission look safe corrected alongside.

THE REGRESSION IS BUILT SO IT CANNOT PASS VACUOUSLY, which is the part worth keeping because the obvious version of this test does pass vacuously. It drives the REAL provider swap path and asserts the DOM element is identical? across the swap BEFORE concluding anything — so a test that silently remounted, rather than swapping, fails instead of reporting success. It carries its own negative control (the original deps vector, marked ^:lint/disable) failing in the bead's exact shape. And it CLEARS THE FIXTURE'S AMBIENT :rf/default DYNAMIC SCOPE: without that, use-frame's dynamic-var tier masks the provider entirely and the whole suite passes while testing nothing. That last one is the trap — an ambient default that makes a frame-isolation test green for the wrong reason.

Gates: uix artefact suite 4 tests / 34 assertions exit 0; check_readme_links.py --ci exit 0. The :browser-test lane is the only one executing the new CLJS test and was NOT run locally (a heavyweight gate wedges rather than fails with siblings live); CI owns it and the PR body declared that reliance. Compensating checks were done rather than assumed: CLJS reader validation of the file, and reading UIx 1.4.4's linter source directly to confirm find-free-variables is locals-only (so test atoms are not flagged) and that use-ref is in stable-hooks (so ref is not demanded as a dep, matching the README).

FOLLOW-UP FROM THE SAME BRANCH, recorded so it is not lost: the require-alias ratchet bounced this PR because both new test files used non-canonical aliases. The fix worker found TWO surfaces over floor, not the one my brief quoted from the CI log — implementation/adapters +2 AND implementation/epoch +3 — and landed both exactly at floor. Had it fixed only the surface I named, the gate would have stayed red. That correction is on rf2-3udw.

title: test-quiet CLJS var-filter regression tests only a copied predicate
description:
## Correctness finding

The CLJS shadow-node contract suite's `find-matching-test-vars-filtering` test does not execute `re-frame.test-quiet.shadow-node/find-matching-test-vars`. It tests a local copy of the predicate, so the advertised namespace-versus-qualified-var selection contract can break while the named regression remains green.

## Evidence

- `implementation/test-quiet/src/re_frame/test_quiet/shadow_node.cljs:173-180` is the production selector. It reads `env/get-test-vars` and filters simple symbols by namespace and qualified symbols by fully-qualified var name.
- `implementation/test-quiet/test/re_frame/test_quiet_shadow_node_cljs_test.cljs:148-175` explicitly says it cannot inject the registry, then defines a local `select` function at lines 157-166 that reproduces the production predicate. The assertions call only that local function; the test namespace cannot require the `:dev/always` runner because doing so forms the documented compile cycle.
- The parser assertions at lines 49-65 prove only that `--test=my.ns/a-test` becomes a symbol. `unmatched-selectors-guard` at lines 191-226 starts from an already-selected `matched-vars` collection. Neither reaches the production filter.
- The process-level `spawn-runner` calls at lines 487-756 use valid namespace selectors or deliberately absent selectors. None selects an existing fully-qualified var, and no process row proves that a namespace selector returns all vars in that namespace.
- Repository-wide `--test=` consumer searches likewise found operational scripts selecting namespaces, not a valid `ns/var`; the only positive qualified-var examples are parser/copy assertions in this test file. A production mutation that ignores `test-var-syms`, treats qualified symbols as namespace symbols, or selects only one var per namespace does not affect the local `select` function and is not discriminated by the process rows.
- Git blame/history shows the copied test was introduced in `953dffc80d` and has never called the production selector. Searches across all bead states/fields for `find-matching-test-vars`, `var filtering`, `fake-var`, `copied predicate`, `shadow-node filtering`, and the test name found no existing issue.

## Impact

The suite reports direct coverage of a supported CLI contract that it does not execute. A regression can make focused single-var runs select nothing or the wrong tests while the parser, copied unit test, unmatched-selector unit test, and ordinary whole-namespace process rows stay green. This is especially hazardous because focused runs are used to reduce large consolidated builds.

## Proposed disposition

Move the pure selection decision into the compile-cycle-safe `re-frame.test-quiet.shadow-node-cli` namespace (for example, a helper accepting `test-syms` and a supplied var collection), make `shadow-node/find-matching-test-vars` delegate to it with `env/get-test-vars`, and point the existing synthetic-var assertions at that shared production helper. An equivalent injectable seam is acceptable, but do not retain a second handwritten predicate in the test. Add one real focused `ns/var` process proof if the cost is acceptable; the shared-helper test is the minimum non-vacuous pin.

## Risks / retained contracts

Do not make the test namespace require `re-frame.test-quiet.shadow-node`; its `:dev/always` test-data macro dependency creates the compile cycle this split exists to avoid. Preserve input order, namespace-wide selection, exact qualified-var selection, mixed selectors, metadata shape (`{:ns :name}`), the unmatched-selector refusal, and the existing public CLI spelling.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `find-matching-test-vars-filtering` in the consolidated test-quiet Node suite and confirm it passes.
2. In a disposable branch, change production `shadow-node/find-matching-test-vars` so either qualified symbols no longer match fully qualified var names or simple symbols no longer select a namespace.
3. Rerun `find-matching-test-vars-filtering`; it still passes because the assertions invoke the test-local `select` predicate rather than the mutated production function.
4. Search the process-level rows for a successful existing `--test=namespace/var` selection; none provides a positive production-path control for the qualified-symbol branch.
5. Restore the mutation after observing the false green.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The var-filtering test invokes the same selection function used by `shadow-node/find-matching-test-vars`; it contains no local copy of the namespace/FQN predicate.
2. Tests cover a namespace selecting every matching var, an existing qualified symbol selecting exactly one var, mixed namespace/FQN selection, and absent selectors.
3. A controlled mutation that removes either the simple-symbol branch or the qualified-symbol branch makes the focused test fail.
4. The `:dev/always` runner remains out of the test namespace's require graph, and the consolidated node-test build compiles without a cycle.
5. A valid namespace-focused real runner still exits 0, an unmatched selector still exits nonzero, and (if added) a real existing `ns/var` selector runs exactly the requested test.
close_reason: PR #9120. Premise held. The rule moved to shadow-node-cli/select-matching-test-vars (the compile-cycle-safe ns unmatched-selectors already lives in) and find-matching-test-vars now delegates to it over env/get-test-vars; the test drives the shipped function and the copy is gone. Plants: removing the simple-symbol branch reds find-matching-test-vars-filtering at :184/:190; removing the qualified-symbol branch reds it at :187/:190 and the FQN selector then matches nothing at the real runner. Control fired: the identical whole-ns invocation on the restored tree reports 0 failures for that row vs 2 under the plant. Added the optional real ns/var process row - the green fixture ns now carries two tests so the namespace selector must see 'Ran 2 tests' and the qualified selector 'Ran 1 tests'. NOTE: driving the shipped selector immediately exposed a real defect, fixed in the same PR - (symbol <ns-symbol> <name-symbol>) keeps both parts unconverted and CLJS hashes a symbol by hashing those parts as strings, so every such symbol hashes to one constant while staying = to the reader's ns/name; a set matched it while array-map-backed (<=8) and stopped above that, so --test= selected correctly up to eight qualified selectors and NOTHING at nine (measured: 8 of 9 real vars reported unmatched). Both call sites now route through one test-var-names helper; the regression pins nine selectors.

title: pair-mcp tests: make the second nREPL candidate regression case reachable
description:
## Finding
One Pair-MCP nREPL regression test contains two independent `cljs.test/async` forms in a single `deftest`. ClojureScript runs only the first async branch, so the `.nrepl-port` fallback assertions in the second branch are unreachable.

## Evidence
- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test/re_frame2_pair_mcp/nrepl_test.cljs`, test `discover-port-shadow-probe-surfaces-each-candidate-file`, has a first async block for `.shadow-cljs/nrepl.port` at lines 776-795 and a second async block for `.nrepl-port` at lines 796-814.
- `clj-kondo --lint tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test` reports `multiple-async-in-deftest` at line 797: only the first async test of a deftest will run.
- The test name and comments promise coverage of each candidate-file probe, but the second branch cannot contribute assertions or a failure.
- Git blame traces this shape to commit `8b65440c7f4`; repository/bead searches found no existing issue for this unreachable branch.

## Impact
A regression in `.nrepl-port` probe-error reporting can pass the suite because its claimed test never executes. This weakens confidence in a live, documented port-discovery fallback.

## Proposed disposition
Either split the two candidate cases into separate `deftest`s or sequence both cases under one `async`/`done` lifecycle. Make execution of both cases observable so the test cannot silently regress to one branch again.

## Risks / retained contracts
Retain both `.shadow-cljs/nrepl.port` and `.nrepl-port` discovery behavior; both are active compatibility paths, not removal candidates. Avoid timing-dependent assertions.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Both candidate-file probe-error cases execute in the test suite and can independently fail.
2. The test uses separate deftests or a single correctly sequenced async lifecycle; no deftest contains multiple sibling `async` forms.
3. `clj-kondo` no longer emits `multiple-async-in-deftest` for `nrepl_test.cljs`.
4. The Pair-MCP test suite passes, including an assertion/counter or equivalent negative-control proof that both candidate branches ran.
notes: AUDIT PR #9076 (2026-09-03): REOPENED. The code split is correct, but the new comment at tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test/re_frame2_pair_mcp/nrepl_test.cljs:776-779 repeats the mechanism this PR and the close reason explicitly disproved: it says ClojureScript runs only the first async form, so the sibling never executes, can never fail, and silently drops assertions. The recorded negative control on the original shape proves the second branch did execute and fail; the actual defect is that it ran outside the awaited lifecycle and lacked independent completion/attribution. Minimal repair: rewrite only this comment to state the real one-async-per-deftest lifecycle reason. No test or production-code redesign is needed.
close_reason: PR #9101 (2026-09-03 15:14 AUSEST). Audit repair as ruled: comment only, no test or production-code change. nrepl_test.cljs:776-779 justified the one-async-per-deftest rule by the DISPROVED mechanism ('ClojureScript runs only the FIRST async form ... a sibling never executes and can never fail'). Rewritten to the real lifecycle reason: a deftest carries ONE async lifecycle, so a sibling async runs OUTSIDE the lifecycle the runner awaits — it DOES execute and its failures DO surface, but with no completion the runner blocks on and no attribution back to the case it covers, so the suite can settle before it finishes and its red can land under the wrong name. The two-deftest split from PR #9076 is untouched and still stands. clj-kondo --lint on the file: exit 0, 0 errors 0 warnings, no multiple-async-in-deftest.

title: bug(skills): implementor filing recipe uses two labels that do not exist upstream
description:
The implementor local filing recipe (skills/re-frame2-implementor/references/cardinal-rules.md, section 8) ends its gh issue create example with:

    --label spec-gap,from-implementor

Neither label exists in day8/re-frame2. Measured live 2026-09-01 from a worker checkout: gh label list --repo day8/re-frame2 returns exactly ten labels (bug, documentation, duplicate, enhancement, good first issue, help wanted, invalid, question, wontfix, nightly-red) and neither spec-gap nor from-implementor is among them.

gh resolves --label names to ids BEFORE the createIssue mutation, so the whole call dies at pre-flight:

    could not add label: spec-gap not found     (exit 1)

Reproduced accidentally while executing the recipe end to end under rf2-2zkrz: the real gh ran instead of a stub, and this is exactly where it stopped. No issue was created -- the pre-flight failure is what saved it, which is also the evidence that filing never reaches the create step.

So the recipe still cannot file even with rf2-2zkrz landed. That bug was the temp-path handoff and its non-goals explicitly fence labels, so this was left standing and filed instead.

Disposition is a real ruling, not a mechanical fix -- pick one:
  1. create the two labels upstream (they are reasonable routing labels for spec gaps from ports), or
  2. drop --label from the recipe entirely, or
  3. point it at an existing label (documentation, or enhancement).

The migration skill recipe (skills/re-frame-migration/references/issue-filing.md) passes no --label at all and is unaffected.

Worth noting the class: nothing gates the recipe against the live repo, which is the same shape of defect as rf2-2zkrz -- the recipe reads correctly and does not run.
notes:
--- MAYOR RULING 2026-09-01 17:55 AUSEST: TAKE OPTION 2, DROP --label ENTIRELY. DISPATCHABLE. ---

Of the three dispositions this item offers, take option 2. Reasons, in the order they decided it:

THE SIBLING RECIPE ALREADY PROVES IT WORKS. skills/re-frame-migration/references/issue-filing.md
passes no --label at all and files successfully. That is not an argument by analogy, it is a working
precedent in this repository on the same surface, and it means option 2 costs nothing that is
currently being had.

routing. Creating spec-gap and from-implementor upstream is an operator action, it makes the recipe
depend on repo state that no gate maintains, and it would put us back here the first time a label is
renamed. It is also the option that cannot be taken by a worker, so choosing it would convert a
dispatchable item into another operator hold.

enhancement, and a wrong label routes worse than an absent one -- it puts the issue in a queue whose
readers will not act on it, which is a silent failure rather than a visible gap.

NOTHING IS FORECLOSED. Dropping the flag leaves label-based routing available the moment somebody
wants it; the labels can be created and the flag re-added in one small change. That asymmetry is why
the smallest option is also the safest here.

EXPLICITLY NOT WANTED, so the next worker does not build it: do NOT add a gate that validates recipe

repo, and right that this is the same shape as rf2-2zkrz -- but the remedy there was a behavioural

offline fixture #8892 added to check_skill_mcp_drift.py, asserting only that the recipe passes no
flag whose value it cannot know is valid.

SCOPE FOR THE DISPATCH: remove --label and its two values from the implementor recipe in
skills/re-frame2-implementor/references/cardinal-rules.md section 8. Confirm at source first that
the two labels really are absent from the repository, since that premise is what makes this a bug
rather than a preference. Re-run the census the item implies -- other pages may carry the same flag.

title: story: variant-share-url appends stale query values instead of replacing them
description:
## Scope

Correct the public tools/story share-URL builder at tools/story/src/re_frame/story/share.cljc and add focused coverage at the builder/browser-consumer seam. The issue is limited to merging Story-owned query keys when variant-share-url receives a base-url that already has a query string.

## Correctness finding

variant-share-url appends its generated query fragments after every existing query fragment. It does not replace an existing value for a key it owns. The browser hydrator reads each key with URLSearchParams.get, whose first-value semantics select the old value. A URL requested for one variant can therefore open a different, stale variant.

This violates the explicit share invariant that a pasted URL lands on the exact same cell. It is a current public-API failure, not malformed-input hardening: variant-share-url publicly accepts base-url, and existing-query merging already has a named test.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Call variant-share-url for :story.new/b with base-url https://example.test/?variant=story.old%2Fa&from=index#/stories.
2. Observe that the returned search string contains variant=story.old%2Fa followed by variant=story.new%2Fb.
3. Construct URLSearchParams from that search string and call get("variant"), exactly as the Story browser hydrator does.
4. Observe story.old/a; share/parse-params therefore restores the old variant, not :story.new/b.

## Evidence

- tools/story/src/re_frame/story/share.cljc:357-370 splits off the hash, detects any question mark, selects ampersand, and concatenates the generated params. It never examines or replaces existing keys.
- tools/story/src/re_frame/story/share.cljc:486-505 exposes that behavior through variant-share-url and always emits the requested variant.
- For base https://example.test/?variant=story.old%2Fa&from=index#/stories and requested variant :story.new/b, the current algorithm produces two variant entries in old-then-new order.
- tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/url_state.cljc:358-384 constructs URLSearchParams and calls .get for variant before share/parse-params. An executable Node URLSearchParams control over the resulting order returns getAll = [story.old/a, story.new/b] but get = story.old/a.
- tools/story/test/re_frame/story_share_test.clj:84-90 covers only an unrelated from=index query and asserts the separator. It has no same-key collision or end-to-end parse assertion.
- tools/story/src/re_frame/story/share.cljc:5-12 and 41-44, tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/url_state.cljc:14-15, and tools/story/spec/005-SOTA-Features.md:203-222 state the invariant: paste/open reproduces the exact cell.

## Failure scenario / invariant

A programmer starts with a URL that already names story.old/a, calls the documented public builder to make a link for story.new/b, and shares the result. The recipient's browser reads the first variant value and hydrates story.old/a. The visible selection is not the requested selection, even though the generated URL also contains story.new/b.

Invariant: for every query key emitted by a variant-share-url call, the returned URL contains one effective value and the real browser parser observes the value generated by that call. Unrelated base query params and the hash route remain intact.

## Recommended minimal fix

Make append-query-params perform a small key-aware merge: before appending generated fragments, remove every existing occurrence of each key emitted by this call, then append one generated value in the current deterministic order. Preserve unrelated query entries, their values, and the fragment. Keep the codec and public signature unchanged; no compatibility layer or forgiving first/last-value parser is needed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Add a focused executable share-builder test whose base contains stale variant and modes values, unrelated from=index and embed=1 values, and #/stories; request a different variant and mode through the real public builder.
- Assert variant and modes each occur exactly once, URLSearchParams.get (or an equivalent standards-faithful browser assertion) returns the newly requested values, and share/parse-params reconstructs those values.
- Assert from=index, embed=1, and #/stories survive unchanged. Retain the existing no-collision existing-query case as the control.
- Demonstrate non-vacuity: the new collision fixture fails against the current append-only implementation because the browser-observed variant is story.old/a; include that red result or an equivalent mutation control in the implementation evidence.
- Run the focused JVM share tests and focused CLJS URL-state/share tests successfully.

## Non-goals

- No URL vocabulary redesign, route redesign, new state slots, parser precedence workaround, compatibility aliases, or broad query-library abstraction.
- No changes to unrelated URL-state hydration/default semantics.
- No normalization of unrelated third-party query parameters.

## Related / duplicate search

Searched all-status bead titles and descriptions for share, URL, variant-share-url, URLSearchParams, duplicate query, stale variant, base-url, existing query, and append-query-params. No issue owns this collision. The returned share-related hits concern shared files/scratchpads/native-share and are unrelated.
acceptance_criteria: A focused test builds from a base containing stale variant/modes plus unrelated from/embed params and a hash route; the result has exactly one value for each emitted Story key, browser first-value parsing and share/parse-params recover the newly requested state, and unrelated params/hash survive. The fixture is shown red against the current append-only implementation (or by an equivalent mutation control), the pre-existing no-collision merge case remains green, and focused JVM plus CLJS share/url-state tests pass.

title: http: abort during body preparation can still issue the JVM request
description:
## Scope

The managed HTTP request lifecycle in `implementation/http`, specifically the boundary from body-thunk realization / encoding to the JVM `HttpClient.sendAsync` call. Cover the shared CLJC lifecycle only as needed to keep its cancellation semantics coherent; keep the public API unchanged.

## Correctness finding

An abort can win while `run-attempt!` is blocked in the managed request-preparation phase, deliver the canonical cancelled reply, and clear the in-flight registry, yet the same attempt proceeds to call `jvm-fetch` after preparation returns. On the real JVM adapter that call invokes `HttpClient.sendAsync`, so a side-effecting request can begin after the framework has told the app it was cancelled.

## Evidence

- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc:1810-1825` checks `@finalised?` only before `prepare-body!`; a body thunk may block inside that call. The successful-preparation branch then enters the host transport with no second cancellation check (`cljs-fetch` at 1827; `jvm-fetch` at 1884).
- The abort closure at `transport.cljc:1658-1718` flips `aborted?`, wins `finalised?`, clears the registry, and dispatches the aborted outcome. During preparation the JVM `cf-holder` is still nil, so it has no future to cancel.
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport_jvm.cljc:285-290` calls `HttpClient.sendAsync` synchronously inside `jvm-fetch`; the returned future is not published to `cf-holder` until `transport.cljc:1911`, after the request has already been issued.
- Deterministic no-network probe at `dba7835137e7`: run `run-attempt!` on a future with a body thunk held by a promise; wait for thunk entry; call `registry/abort-in-flight!`; then release the thunk while `jvm-fetch` is redefined to increment a counter. Observed `:registered-before-abort true`, `:abort-result true`, `:fetch-calls 1`, `:registered-after false` (process exit 0). The cancellation succeeded observably, but transport issuance still followed it.
- `implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_body_prep_failure_test.clj` covers prep throws, encoding failures, and prep retry, but no abort during preparation. `http_abort_retry_race_test.clj` covers retry/backoff handoffs, not the preparation-to-send handoff.
- Spec 014 says body realization is a managed phase that respects abort precedence (`spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:218`) and that a cancelled request must not issue a fresh attempt (`spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:491-499`). The user guide calls manual abort an explicit “stop now” (`docs/async/http.md:306-316`).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build a JVM `run-attempt!` context with a stable `:request-id` and a `:body` thunk that signals entry, then waits on a latch/promise.
2. Start the attempt on another thread and wait for the thunk-entry signal, proving preparation is in progress and the handle is registered.
3. Call `registry/abort-in-flight!` for that id and require it to return true; verify the registry slot is gone.
4. Release the thunk. Instrument or redefine `transport-jvm/jvm-fetch` with a call counter.
5. Current result: the counter becomes 1 even though abort completed before body preparation returned. As a non-vacuity control, omit the abort and observe the same harness call the transport once.

## Failure scenario / invariant

A JVM/SSR app lazily materializes a large upload or signed POST body in a thunk. While that work is running, the user cancels, a resource owner releases, an actor is destroyed, or the frame is torn down. The app receives cancellation (or stale suppression) and the registry reports no live work, but the POST starts afterward and may commit server-side.

Invariant: once an abort has completed before host transport issuance begins, that attempt must never subsequently call the host transport. If issuance wins first, the future must be published before the abort returns so the abort path can cancel it. Exactly one terminal outcome remains observable.

## Recommended minimal fix

Extend the existing cancellation-safe handoff through request preparation and JVM future publication. Re-check the shared `aborted?` / `finalised?` state immediately after successful preparation and skip host transport when cancellation already won. On the JVM, serialize the tiny check → `sendAsync` → `cf-holder` publication region with the abort path (or an equivalent one-cell phase CAS) so there is no residual check-to-send window: abort-before-send suppresses issuance; send-before-abort publishes the cancellable future before abort completes. Apply the shared post-prep guard to CLJS as well for a re-entrant external abort fired by body realization. Reuse the current abort closure, reply CAS, registry cleanup, and reply shapes; add no public surface.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A deterministic JVM regression test uses latches/promises, not timing sleeps, to hold a body thunk in preparation; an abort that returns true before release yields zero `jvm-fetch` / `sendAsync` calls, exactly one canonical `:status :cancelled` reply for manual abort (or the existing suppression outcome for lifecycle abort), and an empty registry.
- The same test fails against the pre-fix implementation by observing one host-transport call after abort.
- Non-vacuity control: the identical harness without abort invokes the host transport exactly once and completes normally, proving the test did not merely disable the send branch or fail before preparation.
- A deterministic handoff control covers the opposite ordering: when JVM issuance wins, the future is published/cancellable before abort completes; abort cancels it and still produces no double reply.
- A focused CLJS regression covers a synchronously/re-entrantly fired external signal during body-thunk realization, or the implementation demonstrates why the shared post-prep guard is host-neutral; no Fetch call occurs after that abort.
- Existing body-preparation failure/retry tests, abort-precedence tests, and abort/retry handoff tests remain green.

## Non-goals

- Interrupting or forcibly terminating arbitrary user body-thunk code already running.
- Expanding `:timeout-ms` semantics to govern body-preparation duration.
- Undoing a request after the server has already received it, stronger delivery guarantees, or transactional HTTP.
- New cancellation APIs, new failure categories, compatibility aliases, or broader transport refactoring.

## Related / duplicate search

Scanned all 1,109 current all-status beads via `bd list --all -n 0`, then searched titles, descriptions, and notes for HTTP, managed abort, body thunk, request preparation / `request-prep`, abort precedence, `jvm-fetch`, cancelled request, and fresh attempt. No bead covers this preparation-to-send cancellation hole. The only current HTTP surface-review bead, `rf2-lddbk`, concerns successful response metadata and is distinct. The sole in-progress bead, `rf2-jui1c`, is an unrelated prose sweep and remains untouched. Historical source/test references `rf2-065xo` (managed prep failures) and `rf2-6nczv9` (retry/backoff cancellation handoffs); neither current tracker record exists, and their shipped tests do not cover abort during body preparation.
notes:
AUDIT PR #8842 (2026-09-01): The post-body-prep gate fixes the named held-thunk ordering, but the required JVM issuance handoff remains incorrect. transport.cljc:1909 CASes issue-phase to :issued before any host side effect; the test seam at :issue/before-send (1910) can then run abort synchronously. That abort returns true, wins finalised?, dispatches the canonical cancelled reply, and clears the registry while cf-holder is still nil. Execution then continues to jvm-fetch/sendAsync at 1969 and only publishes/cancels the future at 1996-2012. A cancel after sendAsync cannot prevent a side-effecting POST from reaching the server, so the framework can still issue the request after abort completed and told the app it was cancelled. The new residual-window test codifies the defect by requiring fetch-calls = 1; it contradicts this bead's invariant/acceptance that, when issuance wins, the cancellable future is published before abort returns. Narrow fix: handshake or serialize actual host entry + future publication with abort (or let an abort before the actual call win and suppress it), and make the deterministic test prove no send occurs after abort completion rather than blessing post-abort send-then-cancel.
AUDIT RESIDUAL REPAIRED — PR #8859 (2026-09-01 12:1x AUSEST). The audit's structural claim held at trunk tip f902e800cc, re-verified in the worktree: the CAS to :issued sat ~60 lines above the jvm-fetch/sendAsync call and ~90 above the cf-holder publication, so an abort in that window lost the cell (could not suppress the send), found cf-holder nil (had nothing to cancel), and completed anyway — registry cleared and canonical cancelled reply delivered — after which the request was issued.

Design chosen: the audit's FIRST shape (serialize host entry + future publication with abort), not the second. The second shape alone — let an abort before the actual call win and suppress it — only shrinks the window: moving the CAS adjacent to the call still leaves a concurrent abort losing the CAS with nothing published to cancel, which is the same defect one step smaller. The bead's invariant ('if issuance wins first, the future must be published before the abort returns') is a mutual-exclusion statement, and only a handshake can make it true. So: the commit CAS is now the first act inside each host's own entry region, and on the JVM that region — CAS, jvm-fetch, reset! cf-holder — is held under a new per-attempt monitor issue-lock that the abort closure's cancel step also takes. Abort-first wins the cell and nothing is sent; abort-during cannot complete (it parks before its cancel step, so registry clear and reply follow the region) and finds the future published. The dead post-publication residual re-check is removed. No app code runs inside the monitor: .whenComplete, clear-in-flight! and dispatch-aborted! are all outside it.

CLJS production semantics are unchanged and need no monitor — single-threaded host, CAS immediately before cljs-fetch, so the only interleaving that host can produce (re-entrant external abort during body realization) is still ordered by the cell; the existing test (3) drives that ordering through the JVM's copy. No public API change, no spec edit: Spec 014 :218/:414/:493-497 already mandate the fixed behaviour and nowhere bless send-then-cancel (checked at source).

The defect-blessing test was FLIPPED and RENAMED, not deleted: abort-in-residual-publish-window-still-cancels-future (asserted fetch-calls = 1 after a completed abort) is now abort-completing-at-issuance-boundary-issues-no-request (asserts ZERO fetch calls and that no future was ever created). New sibling concurrent-abort-cannot-complete-while-host-call-is-in-flight covers the opposite ordering as a live handshake: the jvm-fetch stub runs inside the region, starts a competing abort, observes it reach BLOCKED on the monitor, and samples registry+replies while it is parked (both prove the abort had not completed).

Gates from implementation/http, foreground, exit captured in the same shell: full clojure -M:test exit 0, 508 tests / 3881 assertions, 0 failures. Non-vacuity control — the same namespace against the pre-fix transport.cljc restored from the merge base — exit 1 with exactly the audit's four failures (fetch-calls 1 not 0; a CompletableFuture completed exceptionally by CancellationException where none should exist; observed-blocked false; registry ALREADY EMPTY while sendAsync ran). Heavy CLJS/browser lanes are CI's; the file was reader-checked under both :clj and :cljs feature sets.
