## Simpler elegant target

**Addressing: an actor's address is its id. You either chose it or were handed it.**

```clojure
;; spawn-spec keys (both :spawn and :spawn-all children), closed vocabulary:
{:machine-id | :definition   ;; what
 :data                       ;; map or (fn [{:keys [snapshot event]}] …)
 :start                      ;; first event (else synthetic [:rf.machine.spawn/spawned])
 :id-prefix                  ;; allocated address base            — OR —
 :fixed-actor-id             ;; the literal address (the one stable-name mechanism)
 :on-done  :on-error         ;; completion (see below)
 :id}                        ;; :spawn-all only — the join-name
```

- Parent reads `(get-in data [:rf/spawned <invoke-id>])` (or the `{child-id actor-id}` map for `:spawn-all`); child reads `:rf/self-id` / `:rf/parent-id`. **One send verb:** `[:dispatch [id ev]]`.
- Need a well-known name any sibling can reach? `:fixed-actor-id :primary-request` — the name IS the address, dispatch to it, and a dispatch to a dead one is `:rf.error/no-such-handler` (loud). This is XState `systemId`'s *behaviour* — a stable address reachable by any participant — without a second registry.

**Deletion list (addressing):** `:system-id` spawn key · `re-frame.machines/machine-by-system-id` (both arities) · `:rf.machine/dispatch-to-system` fx + `dispatch-to-system-fx` · `[:rf.runtime/machines :system-ids]` slot (Conventions:595,612; Spec-Schemas:2935) · traces `:rf.machine/system-id-bound` / `-released` (009:187,228) · `:rf.error/system-id-collision` (009:2040) · `:system-id` tag on `:rf.machine.lifecycle/spawned` and `:rf.machine.spawn/spawned` · 5 conformance fixtures · `dispatch_to_system_fx_cljs_test.cljc` and the system-id arms of ~26 other test files · manifest rows `machine-by-system-id` (:1641) and `dispatch-to-system-fx` (:1658 — mis-tiered `:advanced` beside its `:implementation` siblings `spawn-fx`/`destroy-machine-fx` regardless). ~151 source lines in `implementation/machines/src`.

**Deletion list (id-recording):** `:on-spawn` · `:on-spawn-actions` · `:rf.warning/on-spawn-return-ignored` · `:rf.machine.spawn/on-spawn` action-id · 005 §"Recording the spawned id user-side" collapses from four numbered mechanisms to one sentence ("the reducer binds it under `:rf/spawned`; the same fact is at `[:rf.runtime/machines :spawned parent invoke-id]` for tools"). Logging a spawn is what the two `spawned` traces are for.

**Deletion list (phantom):** `:child-machine` — API.md:952 row, 005:4591-4600 "Declarative state-scoped child machines", 005:4635 bullet. 005:4046 already says the thing it describes is `:spawn`.

**Completion: one signal.** A child says "done" by entering a `:final?` leaf (`:output-key` selects the result; `:error? true` marks failure). The runtime already emits `:rf.machine/done` with `:parent-id` and holds `:rf/invoke-id` + `:rf/spawn-all-child-id` at finalize time — so a `:spawn-all` join should consume THAT, not a parent-chosen keyword the child must hand-dispatch:

```clojure
;; before (worker.cljs:303 + child action :dispatch-done)
:spawn-all {:children […] :join :all
            :on-child-done :work/child-done :on-child-error :work/child-error
            :on-all-complete [:work/all-done] :on-any-failed [:work/any-failed]}
;; child: :done {:entry (fn [{data :data}] {:fx [[:dispatch [parent-id [:work/child-done (:shard data)]]]]})}

;; after
:spawn-all {:children […] :join :all
            :on-all-complete [:work/all-done] :on-any-failed [:work/any-failed]}
;; child: :done {:final? true :output-key :result}
```

Delete `:on-child-done` / `:on-child-error`; the child no longer knows its parent's vocabulary, a `:spawn` child and a `:spawn-all` child are the same machine, and `deep_machine`'s double-protocol child becomes one line. **Flag:** this retires the `:rf.machine/join-dispatch` transport and the exact-attempt fold fence built to authenticate child-originated carriers (join.cljc, reply.cljc:285-360, 005:3874) — a design ruling, not a mechanical delete; the runtime-originated `:rf.machine/done` signal is already exact-incarnation fenced by `finalize.cljc`.

**Registration:** teach two doors — `reg-machine` and `defmachine`+`reg-machine`. `reg-machine*` stays (Story's provenance case is real; the macro/fn twin question is `registration-spellings.md`'s). `make-machine-handler` stays as the Level-2 *testing* factory but leaves every registration table (API.md:33,941; 005:945); migrate its two registration-door consumers to `reg-machine`.

**Spawn:** `[:rf.machine/spawn]` stays — it is the desugar target (Data before magic: the runtime and the tools see only the lowered form) and the only non-state-bound lifetime. But 005:2705's heading "Spawning from inside an action (the common case)" is measured false (0 vs 4 declarative + 3 testbed); flip the teaching order and rewrite its example without `:system-id`.

## Why this is better (ethos)

- **Identity is carried, not found** (002's frame rule; Principles §Low hidden context). A per-frame reverse index consulted at send time is ambient lookup creeping back into a system whose stance is that identity travels as a value in the snapshot. Every real consumer discovered this and holds the id.
- **No silent swallow** (Principles:81). `dispatch-to-system` no-ops when unbound — "the caller sees success, the value vanishes" is the text of the principle it violates. `:fixed-actor-id` fails loud via `no-such-handler`.

- **The demand bar** (Principles:124): "a public surface ships only for a named consumer … a capability with no consumer today is parked." This family has had zero consumers across ~30 registered machines and every child-spawning example since it shipped. Parity is behavioural (Mike, 2026-06-22): an addressing *mode* nobody addresses with is not parity, it is surface — and the behaviour (a stable, sibling-reachable address) survives in `:fixed-actor-id`.
- **Data before magic.** `:on-spawn` is a callback whose one plausible output (the id) the runtime refuses, then warns about. The data path (`:rf/spawned`) is the same fact with no callback, no warning, no four-way "which mechanism" section.
- **One protocol for one fact.** A child finishing is one event in the world; XState routes it through `done` for every invoked actor. Two spellings (`:final?` vs "dispatch your parent's keyword") mean a reusable child must implement both — the double-protocol child in `deep_machine` is the smell made concrete.
- **Clojure:** values over registries; one verb with uniform semantics over per-target verbs; delete the phantom so the spec describes only what exists.
- **Honest costs:** the join-transport retirement is real engineering (join.cljc is 1220 lines) and the reply-envelope fold fence was built for good reasons (delayed-dispatch replay); the completion collapse should be its own ruled bead, not bundled with the addressing deletions. `:fixed-actor-id` on re-entry reuses the same id (spawn.cljc:1184) where `:system-id` rebound to a fresh one — the work-generation stamp (spawn.cljc:313) already disambiguates incarnations, but a port must carry that.

## Codex cross-check (2026-09-05 11:07:23 AUSEST)

[`../codex/machine-child-completion.md`](../codex/machine-child-completion.md) took the completion-protocol collapse from this doc, checked it against `finalize.cljc` and `join.cljc`, and calls it the strongest compositional improvement in either corpus: a child finishes by reaching a `:final?` state whether its parent used `:spawn` or `:spawn-all`, and the parent selects the join and its own continuations (`:join :all`, `:on-all-complete`, `:on-any-failed`) without the child knowing that vocabulary. Three corrections to this doc's sketch are adopted:

1. **`:rf.machine/done` is a diagnostic trace, not a join input.** Finalization emits it; nothing consumes it as control. The unified path must route both completion paths through runtime-owned completion processing and emit the observability record from that result. Do not implement the fold by listening to traces.
2. **The exact-attempt coordinates are causal correlation, not authentication.** `join.cljc` says so itself. Preserve them inside the unified path so a stale or replayed result still folds once against the current logical child and attempt; do not describe them as a security fence, and do not import ceremony to protect them.
3. **Finality tears the child down immediately; a joined child today can report done and live on.** The worker and boot examples treat done as terminal, so make that meaning explicit and check their cleanup; progress messages stay ordinary messages and are never reinterpreted as finality.

Codex bounds its finding to terminal completion and says it can ship on its own; the `:system-id` deletion, the registration doors and ad-hoc spawn lifetime are separate questions it neither verified nor refuted. That is the right sequencing: completion unification first as a two-reviewer finding, the `:system-id` deletion as its own one-reviewer ruling.

## Grok Thoughts

**Bother handling?** Yes, two different findings glued together. Child completion is a compositional defect: a reusable worker must know its parent's `:on-child-done` keyword. The `:system-id` family is a parked surface whose park lapsed when rf2-2hpxo closed without it — ~151 lines, five fixtures, zero call sites, and `dispatch-to-system` no-ops when unbound (No silent swallow). `:on-spawn` exists to have its return dropped and a warning emitted. `:child-machine` is a spec row with no implementation.

**Diagnosis.** Addressing is right. Completion is the stronger finding, and Codex's three corrections are load-bearing, not polish:

1. `:rf.machine/done` is a diagnostic *trace*. Do not implement the join by listening to it. Route both paths through runtime-owned completion processing; emit the observability record from that result.
2. Exact-attempt coordinates are causal correlation, not authentication. Keep them so a stale/replayed result folds once against the current logical child and attempt.
3. `:final?` tears the child down immediately; today's joined children can report done and live on. Make "done means terminal" explicit, check worker/boot cleanup, and leave progress as ordinary messages.

The doc's sketch that "the join should consume `:rf.machine/done`" is therefore the one part of the diagnosis that must not be implemented as written.

**Options.** Wave 2 parked the fx "until the facade audit." That audit happened and did not touch this. Keeping it parked again is how parked surfaces become permanent. `:fixed-actor-id` already provides XState `systemId`'s *behaviour* (a stable, sibling-reachable address) without a reverse index, and a dispatch to a dead one is `:rf.error/no-such-handler` (loud). The remaining behavioural difference — `:system-id` rebound to a fresh actor on re-entry, `:fixed-actor-id` reuses the id — is already disambiguated by the work-generation stamp. Ports must carry that stamp; do not pretend the two are identical without it.

**Recommendation.** Three beads, do not bundle.

1. **Completion unification (two-reviewer, first).** A child finishes by entering `:final?` (`:output-key` / error-terminal) under both `:spawn` and `:spawn-all`. Delete `:on-child-done` / `:on-child-error`. Parent keeps `:join`, `:on-all-complete`, `:on-any-failed`. Runtime delivers the result. Migrate `boot.cljs`, `worker.cljs`, `deep_machine` (the double-protocol child becomes one line). Acceptance: one reusable child under both parents; progress, success/error, all/any, cancel/restart, cleanup, recorded/replayed completion.
2. **Addressing deletions (one-reviewer, second).** Delete `:system-id`, `machine-by-system-id`, `:rf.machine/dispatch-to-system`, the `:system-ids` slot, the two traces, the collision error. Teach `:fixed-actor-id` + held `:rf/spawned` / `:rf/self-id` / `:rf/parent-id`. Fix the three drifts even if this bead waits: Conventions.md:441 still names the deleted fn; 009:2138 contradicts 005:2999; the migration skill tells people to use `:system-id` while Pattern-Boot says not to.
3. **`:on-spawn` and `:child-machine`.** Delete. The reducer already binds the id. The phantom spec row has described `:spawn` since 005:4046.

Leave destroy's four reasons, `:raise`, `:spawn` vs `[:rf.machine/spawn]` (desugar target), and the `reg-machine`/`defmachine` pair. Sweep the two testbed `make-machine-handler` compositions onto `reg-machine`; reorder 005 §Registration so the macro leads.

**Implement.** Join.cljc is 1220 lines — completion is real engineering, not a rename. Chain after any still-open reply-envelope work that touches `reply.cljc`. Do not listen to traces. Do not describe the fold fence as a security boundary.

## Codex Thoughts

**Verdict: terminal child-completion unification is a strong compositional improvement. The system-id deletion is a separate, less-settled capability decision, and its claimed replacement is not behaviorally equivalent.**

The newer cross-check correctly repairs the original completion sketch: `:rf.machine/done` is an observability record, not a control channel. Runtime completion processing must produce the parent result and the trace; it must not subscribe to traces to drive joins.

The useful target is narrow: **a terminal child should not need to know whether its parent used `:spawn` or `:spawn-all`.** The [long-running worker](../../../../examples/patterns/long_running_work/worker.cljs) currently announces its parent's join keyword manually, and the [boot example](../../../../examples/patterns/boot/boot.cljs) follows the same pattern. A reusable child reaching a final success/error state should be sufficient for either parent form.

However, joining a reported result and terminating an actor are not the same event. Today, a child can report a milestone and remain alive; `:final?` initiates teardown. Make terminal completion the intended meaning for the supplied boot/worker examples, and check that no subsequent behavior depends on those children remaining available. Progress and nonterminal milestones remain ordinary events. Do not add a general completion-policy language to cover hypothetical future uses.

For implementation, converge [`finalize.cljc`](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/finalize.cljc) and [`join.cljc`](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/join.cljc) on a runtime-owned result-processing path that preserves parent/invoke/logical-child/attempt correlation. Preserve duplicate suppression, superseded-attempt rejection, parent-exit behavior, and join policy outcomes. These coordinates support causality and correct lifecycle handling; they are not an application authentication protocol. Retire the public child-chosen completion keywords only after terminal success, terminal error, retry, and child teardown demonstrate equivalent intended outcomes.

**Do not substitute `:fixed-actor-id` for `:system-id` on an equivalence claim.** [`spawn.cljc`](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/spawn.cljc) allocates actor identity separately from the reverse-index binding, and system-name collisions rebind the name. A stable name can therefore point to a new actor while an earlier actor retains its own identity. A fixed address instead reuses the identity itself. The work-generation stamps already used by lifecycle machinery do not establish that every ordinary application dispatch carries incarnation information.


Three options deserve an explicit choice: retain named addressing as a small advanced capability; deliberately de-scope it because it has no named application consumer; or require applications to carry identities and own any rebinding they need. The latter two can be sensible pre-alpha decisions, but neither preserves every named-addressing behavior automatically. My recommendation is to ship the terminal-completion simplification independently and not make that valuable change depend on settling the address-family question.

Removing the unused `:on-spawn` authoring hook and correcting phantom `:child-machine` documentation are plausible smaller follow-ups. Preserve explicit spawn/destroy operations and `make-machine-handler`'s pure-testing role. Their different ownership and execution roles are useful distinctions, not additional aliases to eliminate for the sake of a lower count.

# Machine children: finish the same way under one parent or a join

Review date: 2026-09-05. Status: proposal only. Bead: `rf2-snkw`.

New understanding from [Fable's machine lifecycle review](../fable/machine-child-lifecycle-and-addressing.md), checked against child examples and the finalize/join implementations. This is its strongest compositional improvement; it need not be bundled with every proposed machine-surface deletion.

## Finding

A child under `:spawn` can finish by entering a `:final?` state, selecting a result with `:output-key`; the runtime handles completion and teardown. Under `:spawn-all`, examples instead hand-dispatch a parent-selected `:on-child-done` or `:on-child-error` event, including the parent's logical child ID.

Both report terminal child work, but the second convention makes the child know its parent's join vocabulary. Reusing a child under a different parent arrangement therefore requires protocol knowledge unrelated to the work the child performs.

## Known use cases and evidence

| Use case | Source evidence | What must remain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| State-scoped single child | [Websocket connection](../../../../examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs), declarative `:spawn` | Parent state owns child lifetime; leaving the state cancels the child. |
| Single-child success/failure and result selection | [Finalization](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/finalize.cljc) | `:final?`, `:output-key`, error-terminal handling, parent completion logic and cleanup. |
| Fan out work and join its completion | [Long-running work](../../../../examples/patterns/long_running_work/worker.cljs): `:dispatch-done` and `:spawn-all`; [boot](../../../../examples/patterns/boot/boot.cljs) | All/any join decisions, results/failure and the parent's continuation events. |
| Incremental progress before completion | Long-running work's `:process-one` action sends `:progress` | Ordinary child-to-parent messages remain independent of terminal completion. |
| A child already using both conventions | [Deep-machine testbed](../../../../testbeds/deep_machine/core.cljs): final leaf plus explicit child-done dispatch | Avoid double reporting while preserving its finality and cleanup. |
| Late, repeated or cross-attempt completion during cancellation/restart/replay | [Join implementation](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/join.cljc) | A result must belong to the current logical child and attempt, and be folded once. This is ordinary causal correctness in a trusted program. |
| Inspect machine work and join state | [Xray machine inspector](../../../../tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/machine_inspector.cljs) and lifecycle trace consumers | Retain meaningful child status, join progress and terminal records; tools should not require the old app-chosen completion keyword. |

## Proposed smaller API

Let a child finish by reaching a final state regardless of whether its parent used `:spawn` or `:spawn-all`:

```clojure
;; PROPOSED as the universal child-completion convention.
;; Child: result is already stored under :result in its data.
:done {:final? true :output-key :result}

;; Parent: selects a join and its own continuations, not the child's vocabulary.
:spawn-all {:children children
            :join :all
            :on-all-complete [:work/all-done]
            :on-any-failed [:work/any-failed]}
```

Remove the join's `:on-child-done` / `:on-child-error` declarations and the terminal hand-dispatch actions from the migrated children. An error final state uses the existing error-terminal convention. Keep progress messages and the parent's domain-specific continuation events; those express different facts.

The runtime already knows the parent, invocation, child membership and attempt. It should use that information to deliver a terminal result to the parent completion handler or join. No new application-visible completion envelope or child-address DSL is needed.

## Important implementation correction to the source proposal

Fable describes feeding the existing `:rf.machine/done` signal into joins. In the inspected implementation, that name is also a diagnostic trace emitted by finalization; it is not an already-working universal join input. Do not implement this by listening to traces. Route both completion paths through runtime-owned completion processing and emit observability records from that result.

The current join's exact-attempt coordinates protect against stale/duplicate completion and support replay. They are explicitly not authentication or a secret capability. Preserve that causal information inside the unified path; trusting the programmer does not make yesterday's asynchronous result belong to today's restarted child.

There is also a real lifetime choice: finality tears down a child immediately, whereas current joined children can report done before the parent reaps them. The cited worker/boot examples treat done as terminal. Make that meaning explicit, check their cleanup, and retain ordinary messages for genuinely non-terminal milestones. Do not silently reinterpret milestone messages as finality.

## Why this is more elegant

A worker should know how to perform and finish its task. A parent should decide how child results combine. One completion convention separates those responsibilities and makes the same child reusable under a single invocation, an all-join or an any-join.

That is substantive compositional power, not cosmetic deletion: fewer facts are duplicated across parent and child. It follows [the project's simple computational model](../../../../spec/000-Vision.md) while preserving ordinary event messaging where it carries real application meaning.

## Focused acceptance evidence

Migrate boot, long-running work and the double-protocol testbed; demonstrate one reusable child under both `:spawn` and `:spawn-all`. Check progress, success/error, all/any joins, cancellation/restart, cleanup and recorded/replayed completion. Keep the work bounded to terminal completion; system IDs, registration macros and ad-hoc spawn lifetime are separate questions.

# Machine messaging — four ways to send an event to a machine

**Status:** medium-high (an entire named-addressing surface with zero consumers; wave 2, 2026-07-10 14:30 AUSEST, Fable-authored)
**Surfaces:** plain `dispatch`/`:dispatch` to a machine/actor id, `:raise`, `dispatch-to-system` (fn, impl tier), `:rf.machine/dispatch-to-system` (fx), the `:system-id` registry behind them

---

## The problem

A machine IS an event handler, so the framework's one send verb already reaches it. Yet the surface
offers four spellings for "send an event to a machine":

| Spelling | What it is |
|---|---|
| `[:dispatch [machine-or-actor-id event]]` (fx) / `dispatch` fn from views | the ordinary send, with the id you hold |
| `:raise` (fx, machine-internal) | self-event, atomic, pre-commit, same macrostep |
| `:rf.machine/dispatch-to-system` (fx) | send by **`:system-id`** — a name registry lookup |
| `dispatch-to-system` (fn, `re-frame.machines`) | the fx's call-site twin, already demoted off the facade |

---

## Empirical use cases

### 1. Feature code → registered machine — **the workhorse**

Dozens of sites: `[:dispatch [:auth/flow [:auth/login draft]]]` (`realworld_http/auth.cljs:286,319,344`),
plus `:ui/nine-states`, `:ws/connection`, `:app/boot`, `:work/flow`, … Machine ids are ordinary
registration ids; the send is ordinary dispatch.

### 2. View → machine

Same thing from UI callbacks: `#(dispatch [:work/flow [:start]])` (`long_running_work/views.cljs:119-127`).

### 3. Child actor → parent, parent → child — **captured ids, always**

Every actor example threads the id as a value: `[:dispatch [parent-id [:ws/opened …]]]`
(`websocket/messages.cljs:276,320`), `[:dispatch [(:parent-id data) [:progress …]]]`
(`long_running_work/worker.cljs:143,152`), boot kick `[:dispatch [:app/boot [:rf.machine/start]]]`.
Spawned-child ids arrive via `:on-spawn` / snapshot data and are *held*.

### 4. Named-target send (`dispatch-to-system` fn + fx)

**Zero call-sites in `examples/` and `tools/`.** Both surfaces live only in `implementation/machines/`
(src + their own tests) and `docs/machines/`. The case they were designed for — messaging a spawned
child without holding its id — is served in every real example by *holding the id*.

### 5. Machine-internal self-event (`:raise`)

Zero example uses; 10 snippets across `docs/machines/`. Semantically distinct from self-dispatch
(atomic, pre-commit, same macrostep — the drain never sees it) and part of the XState parity surface.

---

## Simpler elegant target

### One send verb; hold your ids

1. **Plain dispatch is the machine-messaging story, full stop.** The docs should say it in one line:
   *a machine is an event handler; you message it the way you message anything — dispatch to the id you
   hold.* Actor ids are values you carry (`:on-spawn`, snapshot data), exactly like frame identity.
2. **Delete `dispatch-to-system` (fn).** Zero consumers, already demoted off the facade, and it is the
   call-site twin of the fx — the same redundant-twin shape the corpus has deleted three times already
   (`reg-machine*`, `dispatch*`/`subscribe*`, the sub-sugar family). Pre-alpha, tombstone-free.
3. **`:rf.machine/dispatch-to-system` (fx): keep, parked in place, advanced tier.** The honest tension:
   the demand bar says delete (zero consumers), but XState v6 parity protects the *capability* (actor
   systems address by `systemId`; parity is behavioural, and "message a sibling you didn't spawn" is a
   real statechart pattern this enables). Resolution: it stays the **one** named-addressing surface,
   classified advanced/parity in the manifest, with a recorded demand-note — if the facade audit at
   API-freeze still finds zero consumers, that is the moment to rule on deletion with full information.
   No new twins, no promotion into teaching material meanwhile.
4. **`:raise` unchanged.** It is not a send-to-a-machine overlap; it is the machine's internal grammar
   with semantics dispatch cannot express (pre-commit atomicity). Docs-only usage is fine — it is
   grammar for machine authors, like `:after` or `:always`.

Result: the teaching table has one row (dispatch), one internal grammar note (`:raise`), and one
advanced escape hatch — instead of four apparent peers.

---

## Why this is better (ethos)

**re-frame2:** *identity is carried, not found* (the frame rule, applied to actors). A name registry
consulted at send time is ambient lookup creeping back into a system whose whole stance is that
identity travels as a value. The examples discovered this themselves: every one of them holds the id.

**The VM story:** events are the instruction stream and dispatch is the only way instructions enter.
A second mailbox API for one kind of handler would mean machines are *not* ordinary event handlers —
undoing the single most elegant fact about the machines design.

**Clojure:** prefer values (a held id) over registries (a name looked up elsewhere); prefer one verb
with uniform semantics over per-target verbs.

**Masterpiece:** the strongest feature of this area is what it *doesn't* have — no `send-to-machine`,
no actor mailbox type, no second queue. Protect that by refusing twins, not by growing the exception.

---

## Non-goals

- Do not invent `send-to-machine` or any machine-specific send verb.
- Do not alias `:raise` to self-dispatch (pre-commit atomicity is load-bearing and parity-relevant).
- Do not remove the `:system-id` registry wholesale without checking its read-side consumers
  (`machine-by-system-id`, snapshot `:system-ids`, tool display) — that is the facade-audit question,
  not this doc's.
- Do not touch spawn/join or `:on-spawn` id delivery — they are what makes hold-the-id workable.

## Grok Thoughts

**Bother handling?** Yes. A machine is an event handler; `dispatch` already reaches it. The named-addressing family (`:system-id`, `machine-by-system-id`, `:rf.machine/dispatch-to-system`) had zero consumers in July and still has zero in September. The fn twin is gone, as this doc asked. The fx was parked "until the facade audit." That audit (rf2-2hpxo) closed 2026-09-04 without this surface in scope, so the park is void.

**Diagnosis, in hindsight.** "Identity is carried, not found" was the right law, and every example already obeyed it. Parking the fx for XState `systemId` *parity* was the miss: an addressing mode nobody addresses with is not parity, it is surface. `dispatch-to-system` no-ops when unbound — the principle this doc did not yet cite, and the reason the fx should not have been given another stay.

**What to do now.** Do not implement this doc's "keep the fx, parked, advanced." Implement `machine-child-lifecycle-and-addressing.md`'s deletion list instead: the fx, the lookup, the slot, the traces, the collision error. `:fixed-actor-id` is the stable-name behaviour without a reverse index, and a dispatch to a dead one is loud. `:raise` stays (pre-commit atomicity; not a send-to-machine overlap). Completion unification is a different bead and a better finding — do that first, then delete this family.

**Do not** invent `send-to-machine`. Do not alias `:raise` to self-dispatch. Fix Conventions.md:441 (still names the deleted fn) even if the fx waits one more bead.

## Codex Thoughts

**Verdict: the everyday messaging recommendation is correct and the redundant function has already been removed. Update this dossier's status rather than reopening its July implementation plan.**

Current [`re-frame.machines`](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines.cljc) retains `machine-by-system-id` and the named-addressing effect, but no longer defines the `dispatch-to-system` call-site function. Its source explicitly records that deletion and the advanced/parity rationale for the remaining effect. The original table should therefore be read as historical.

Continue teaching ordinary dispatch to a carried machine or actor id. The [worker](../../../../examples/patterns/long_running_work/worker.cljs) and [websocket connection](../../../../examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs) make that model concrete. For declarative children, the runtime now provides ids through `:rf/spawned`; references here suggesting that `:on-spawn` is how applications obtain them should defer to that data path. No machine-specific mailbox abstraction is needed.

`:raise` remains genuinely different: it participates inside the machine's current macrostep. Replacing it with queued self-dispatch changes atomicity and ordering, even if ordinary examples have not needed it. It is correctly excluded from the duplication finding.


The September lifecycle dossier argues for deleting the remaining named-addressing family. Its absence of application consumers is relevant, but its fixed-id replacement needs correction. A **role name resolved at send time** and an **actor identity retained by a caller** answer different questions. The [spawn implementation](../../../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/spawn.cljc) can rebind a system name while retaining separate generated actor identities; using the role name directly as `:fixed-actor-id` collapses that distinction.

The viable choices are:

- Keep the existing advanced named-send effect and lookup, documenting their late-binding semantics.
- Deliberately stop supporting role-name addressing, with ordinary carried ids as the smaller supported model.
- Move that role registry into application data, accepting application-owned rebinding and the necessary injected inputs for pure handlers.

The third option is not free merely because it uses maps. It transfers lifecycle responsibility to the programmer. Conversely, preserving the advanced capability need not promote it into every introductory example. My recommendation is to keep the current teaching hierarchy and make any capability retirement a separate explicit ruling, not an automatic consequence of counting spellings.

If retained, clarify that an unbound system name currently produces no dispatch; do not describe this as ordinary dispatch's error behavior. Whether to change that policy is its own question, not necessary API cleanup. If retired, verify rebinding, address reuse, and frame isolation before claiming the replacement's semantics.

This is a good place to stop after restoring an accurate account of the current API. The larger ergonomic opportunity is reusable terminal child completion, covered separately, rather than inventing another send grammar.

**Decision needed from Mike:** Whether the three zero-consumer machine surfaces — the `:system-id` reverse-index family, the `:on-spawn` observer hook, and the unimplemented `:child-machine` spec key — are deleted outright, partly parked, or kept as designed.

## The problem

A spawned actor is an event handler whose id is its address (005 §Spawning). Every real parent and child in the tree already holds that id and sends with the one verb. This is the addressing story as practised, at tip:

```clojure
;; examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs:99-108 — parent reads the child's id
;; from its own :data; the reducer bound it there at spawn time (transition.cljc:562).
(def ^:private socket-invoke-id [:active])
(defn- socket-id [data]
  (get-in data [:rf/spawned socket-invoke-id]))

;; examples/patterns/websocket/messages.cljs:342-344 — child reads both ids the
;; spawn fx stamped into its :data and dispatches back.
(let [self-id   (:rf/self-id data)
      parent-id (:rf/parent-id data)] …)

;; examples/patterns/long_running_work/worker.cljs:56,143 — a :spawn-all child
;; names its parent's registered id directly; the one send verb.
(def parent-id … #_"the parent's registered id")
{:fx [[:dispatch [parent-id [:progress shard new-processed (:total data)]]]]}
```

Re-measured at tip across `examples/`: `:rf/spawned` 19 mentions, `:rf/self-id` 15, `:rf/parent-id` 8, `[:dispatch [id …]]` dozens. Beside that story, 005 teaches a second addressing mode — and heads it "the common case":

```clojure

          {:fx [[:rf.machine/spawn {:machine-id :request/protocol
                                    :system-id  :pending-request   ;; address the child by name
```

### The strongest counter-evidence, honestly

Codex's caution, verified in source: **`:system-id` and `:fixed-actor-id` are not behaviourally equivalent**, so "just use `:fixed-actor-id`" is not a drop-in claim. In plain terms:

- **`:fixed-actor-id :x`** — the literal *is* the actor's address (`spawn.cljc:57`). When the parent leaves the state the child is destroyed; on re-entry a *new incarnation* comes up at the *same* address `:x` (`spawn.cljc:1184-1185`: "`:fixed-actor-id` children reuse the SAME id across attempts; `actor-generation` is always 1 for them"). Two live children resolving to one literal are rejected fail-closed (`spawn.cljc:160-210`, `:rf.error/machine-spawn-all-duplicate-id`).
- **`:system-id :x`** — the name is a pointer in a per-frame map; the actor keeps its own gensym'd address. A second spawn under `:x` **rebinds** the pointer to the new actor, last-write-wins, emitting `:rf.error/system-id-collision` (`spawn.cljc:478-490`); the old actor lives on, unnamed, at its own address (005:2903).

So the two differ in exactly one scenario: *"start a fresh actor under a stable role while the previous one keeps running."* Under `:fixed-actor-id` that is an overwrite the runtime refuses; under `:system-id` it is a rebind. The `:work-generation` stamp at `spawn.cljc:313` (`(if (contains? args :fixed-actor-id) (:rf/attempt join-state) (actor-generation spawned-id))`) lets the *join and lifecycle machinery* tell incarnations apart — a completion from a prior incarnation is suppressed `:attempt-superseded` (`join_exact_attempt_cljs_test.cljc:219-225` pins exactly the fixed-id respawn case). But that stamp does not ride on an ordinary application dispatch: an app that dispatches `[:x ev]` after re-entry reaches whichever incarnation currently owns `:x`. Under any delete option, an app wanting "new actor now, old one lingers" must allocate (`:id-prefix`) and hold the id. Nobody in the corpus wants that today.

Two facts bound the counter. First, XState parity is *behavioural, not surface* (Mike, 2026-06-22; EP-0029) — and an addressing mode with zero addressers is surface. Second, and new in this dossier: **the rebind is not XState's behaviour either.** The parity reference's `system._set` throws on a duplicate: `Actor with system ID '${systemId}' already exists.` (fetched from `statelyai/xstate` `main`, `packages/core/src/system.ts`, 2026-09-06). So the one behaviour that distinguishes `:system-id` from `:fixed-actor-id` is a *divergence* from the reference, kept in the name of parity. `:fixed-actor-id`'s "one live actor per literal, loud on collision" is the closer match to `systemId` as XState actually ships it.

## The decision

**Which of these does Mike rule for the three families?**

- **A.** Delete all three: the `:system-id` family, the `:on-spawn` family, the phantom `:child-machine`. The address is the id; `:fixed-actor-id` is the one stable-name mechanism.
- **B.** Delete `:on-spawn` and `:child-machine` now; **park** `:system-id` with a written un-park trigger and promotion shape (Principles §demand bar's park form).
- **C.** Keep all three as designed; fix the drifts only (rf2-kuky.16).

(The bead's description carries codex's lettering — A retain / B de-scope / C app-owns-rebinding; its B and C are the same deletion and are merged into this dossier's **A**.)

### Independently verified findings

My search across executable Clojure/ClojureScript files under `examples`, `testbeds`, `tools`, and `skills` found no application authoring of `:system-id` or `:on-spawn`. The hits are tool vocabulary/projection support, tests, and comments. Thus “two live children resolving to one literal are rejected” and “fixed IDs are the closer collision-policy match” overgeneralize a batch guard. This is source-path analysis, not an executed collision reproduction. Do not sell fixed IDs as universally protected singleton allocation.
2. **Separate identity matters without overlapping lifetimes.** `connection.cljs`'s `from-live-socket?` compares an incoming source ID with the current generated child ID to reject a previous connection's stragglers. Reusing one literal across sequential connections destroys that distinction unless the application adds another generation value. The dossier's “exactly one scenario” is therefore too narrow. Retiring role lookup need not change these consumers at all: retain their generated, carried IDs. Join attempt tokens do not automatically decorate ordinary messages.
3. **`:on-spawn` is not literally a warning-only no-op.** [apply-on-spawn](../../implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/transition.cljc) invokes application code before commit, discards its return, and turns exceptions into machine-action failure. Delete this hook because no demonstrated consumer needs this pre-commit callback and its positioning complicates the otherwise data-oriented fold—not because invoking it can do nothing. Post-drain trace observation is appropriate for diagnostics, not timing-equivalent replacement behavior.

title: RULED: no perf gate now - timing ratio-band unfit; core byte budget awaits a representative app + agreed growth figure
description:
RULED 2026-09-09. No new performance gate is built. This bead is PARKED ON A DECISION, not open on a question — see notes for the full ruling and evidence.

What the old title asserted is no longer true. Three regression gates already exist and must not be re-derived as missing:
- `fresco-bench-compile` (nightly, `expensive-tests.yml:822`, 84 s) — shipped by rf2-a7ds / PR #9533.
- `cljs-schemas-bundle` (`test.yml:3874`) — a real two-sided gzipped byte-margin gate.
- The MCP wire-pipeline benchmark — wall-clock median ceilings asserted per PR via `node-test-tools-re-frame2-pair-mcp` on the `mcp_conformance` surface.

WHAT REMAINS UNCOVERED, and it is narrow: no CI gate compares the core/browser runtime's representative performance across revisions.

RULED OUT PERMANENTLY: any wall-clock RATIO-BAND gate on the browser substrate. Four independent measurements in the notes (37% and 58% floor drift; band wider on an IDLE box, corr(band,floor) = -0.49; a 25% ceiling calibrated never to fire that fired three times in two days; the replacement 35% ceiling's stated 2.7%/run false-fire rate). Do not re-propose one without refuting all four. A COARSE absolute budget with 10-100x headroom is a different thing and is not pre-refuted.

RULED OUT AS SPECIFIED: a byte margin on `re-frame.core`. It gates the volatile quantity itself (that control's own figure moved 50.3 -> 94.1 KB gzipped in under a quarter, all but 1.0 KB of it core), so a ~10% ceiling becomes a recurring threshold bump on deliberate pre-alpha growth — a ratchet, not a gate. The schemas gate already hit exactly this and was rebuilt rather than re-baselined.

TRIGGER TO REOPEN — and it is NOT publication, since a tag supplies neither a workload nor a threshold: (a) a named representative application whose footprint is the budgeted quantity, and (b) an agreed tolerated growth figure. That is already the standing rf2-kybsf ruling. The `rf2-kmqx3` edge is retained for scheduling hygiene only (it keeps a decided-no bead out of `bd ready`); its stated publication rationale is superseded.

Blocking unknown, unchanged: no historical regression a gate would have caught can be named. That remains the strongest reason the answer is "not now".

### THE TIMING-LANE UNFITNESS EVIDENCE — four independent measurements, all re-verified

This is the reusable content of this bead. **Do not re-propose a ratio-band timing gate without first refuting all four.**

1. **Floor drift, same arm, same box.** 4.3 ms -> 5.9 ms across 5 rounds = **37%**, described in place as "larger than most of the effects being measured"; across 12 interleaved rounds, **58%**. Source: `docs/design/freehand/studio/compiled-tier-browser-worth-it.md:112-116` and `:270`. Related: the same primitive read 10.4 ns vs 21.7 ns on two JVMs on one box; a CPU-time split over 3 repeats of one pair gave 1.81 / 0.85 / 1.85 — "a spread like that supports no number".

2. **The calibrated band is HALF AGAIN as wide as the band the ceiling was set above.** A fresh 19-run ladder (0/2/4/8/12/20 competing cores, 24-core box, silent throughout) reads **band 4.4%–31.1%, mean 14.0%, median 11.7%** on raw `TaskDuration`, against the `rf2-cvvb7` calibration's 4.4%–18.5%, mean 8.9%. Frame-only is wider again (4.9%–32.6%, mean 15.3%). "A gate set above the widest of nineteen draws has no margin for the instrument moving, and it moved." Source: `bench/fresco/src/re_frame/bench/fresco/seam.cjs:96-108`.

3. **THE BAND IS WIDEST ON AN IDLE BOX** — the opposite of what was expected, and the single most useful thing the re-take found. By rung: **24.6%** at zero load, then 11.8 / 8.3 / 12.8 / 13.2 / **9.6%** at 2/4/8/12/20 competing cores. **`corr(band, floor) = -0.49`.** Per-sample floor dispersion falls monotonically with load, 30.0% -> 15.2%, while the floor absolute RISES 3.78 -> 6.93 ms. A busy box is slower and STEADIER; an idle one is faster and jumpier, because between samples its cores park, its clock drops, and every sample pays a different wake-up. **Consequence that kills the obvious workaround:** a precondition of the form "adjudicate only when the floor is inside the calibrated range" would refuse the most reproducible runs the instrument can take. Source: `seam.cjs:109-120`.

4. **A ceiling calibrated never to fire FIRED THREE TIMES IN TWO DAYS.** The 25% ceiling was set above nineteen draws and still broke: 26.2% on an earlier `bulk300` ensemble (rf2-yd52q), then 26.2% on `bulk300` and 28.4% on `narrow` in one run of rf2-emvod's. "A threshold that was above nineteen draws of a tail was never above the tail, and roughly one run in eleven crosses it." Its replacement is a **JUDGEMENT-SET 35%**, explicitly not a quantile, carrying a stated **2.7% per-run false-fire rate** against the 25% predecessor's **9.1%**; 2 of 19 re-take runs breach 25%, 0 of 19 breach 35%, both breaches at ZERO load. Source: `seam.cjs:121-134` and `:182`.

**Independent replication, and it holds.** Codex read the archived ladder directly from git (`ladder-ymi6j.json`, blob `e5a4aba448faa0db1cf7b604de4af5a95926ad35` at commit `7b492b98cb`) without restoring the corpus, and reproduced **4.444%–31.083%, mean 13.967%**, 2 runs above 25%, none above 35%; run-preserving resampling at 200,000 draws gave **9.066% above 25% and 2.681% above 35%**. Two instruments, one answer, matching the repo's 4.4–31.1 / 14.0 / 9.1% / 2.7% to three digits.

**Codex's caveat is accepted and recorded honestly:** those percentages estimate rejection under this historical instrument's *noise-admissibility* rule — whether a run supports a reportable magnitude — and are not measured CI false-red rates for a hypothetical comparator. See point 2 of Correction 1.

**Fifth, structural, and it kills a bench-run gate independently of noise:** ruling rf2-6c12m.1 keeps `bench/*` off every per-PR lane because **the bench suites exercise LOCAL COPIES of the runtime** — "running them per PR could not catch a regression in the shipped one" (`.github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh:2570`). The tree also mixes frozen donor implementations with maintained measurement code (`bench/fresco/README.md:75` on). So even a nightly *run* of the lane would not be a regression gate on the shipped artefact until someone establishes which implementation the chosen arm exercises. There is also a stored wall-clock baseline, `clock_check_standard.json`, which discloses its own fatal residual: **commit-level independence has never been measured** — both ensembles were taken in one session ~90 minutes apart on one tree. A baseline never shown to survive a commit boundary cannot judge commits.
### CORRECTION 2 (Codex wins, and it decides the byte question): option C is a RATCHET, not a gate

The dossier proposed cloning `cljs-schemas-bundle` into a `re-frame.core` byte margin. **The source of that pattern already ruled against it, and the arithmetic says why.**

- `implementation/schemas/test/re_frame/schemas_bundle_control.cljs` records the core-growth figure and then says, in terms: *"The figure is recorded and DELIBERATELY left alone: no gate, no remedy. Pre-alpha growth is expected, and per the rf2-kybsf ruling an absolute core budget belongs on a representative app in its own gate if one is ever wanted."* That is a substantive prior decision recorded in source, not a missing checker.
- **The growth rate makes a ceiling unmaintainable.** That control's own quantity — `cljs.core` + `re-frame.core` — measured **50.3 KB gzipped (2026-05-14) -> 94.1 KB (2026-08-05)**, and all but 1.0 KB of the 44.8 KB move was core rather than Malli. A ~10% headroom ceiling on a quantity growing ~87% per quarter fires within weeks, every time as a threshold bump on deliberate expected growth. Under this project's never-a-flake rule nobody may wave it through, so **each bump costs a worker**. That is precisely the ceremony the posture forbids.
- **This is the schemas gate's own history, and the repo already refused to repeat it.** `test.yml:3874`'s comment block: the gate first shipped an ABSOLUTE ceiling, came back RED at 124.9 KB against 100 KB, and *"THE RED WAS NOT A REGRESSION"* — it was `cljs.core` + `re-frame.core` growing 43.8 KB while the schemas surface grew 1.0 KB. **It was not threshold-bumped.** It was rebuilt to assert a differential in which the volatile part cancels: *"Any re-baselined absolute would have been wrong again within a quarter, so the gate now has none."*
- **A `re-frame.core` margin cannot make that volatile part cancel, because the volatile part IS the quantity.** An empty-app control roots almost none of the `cljs.core` that `re-frame.core` pulls in (`cljs/core.cljs` is 186.0 KB of the probe's 494 KB optimized bytes, largely rooted by core), so the subtraction does not cancel it — it measures it. The dossier's claim that the differential "cancels `cljs.core` growth" is the one place the dossier is simply wrong, and it is load-bearing for its recommendation.
- **Two smaller corrections from Codex, both verified and both real.** (i) The control's `boot` is a deliberate no-op while the probe roots four API calls, so the two builds' *executable* difference is not literally one require — the no-op shape is documented as necessary for the control's rooting to stay a strict SUBSET, and copying it to a core probe would measure what the require retains rather than what an app using dispatch and subscriptions costs. (ii) The "zero flakes / ~0.03% spread" reassurance comes from six builds of ONE probe on ONE tree (`check-schemas-bundle.cjs:62`), and neither zero-flake behaviour nor the ~50 s cost is established for a job that does not exist. The checker itself acknowledges extra core paths rooted by schemas (`:67`).

**Where the dossier still wins:** bytes are the right SHAPE for the eventual gate, deterministic quantities do belong in blocking PR gates, and the remaining coverage gap it identifies is real — nothing in CI compares the core/browser runtime's representative performance across revisions. It is the *quantity and the timing* that are wrong, not the instinct.

### THE PATTERN TO CLONE WHEN THE TRIGGER FIRES — kept, so nobody re-derives it

Not authorised now. Recorded because it is the reusable half and re-deriving it costs a day.

- **Exemplar:** job `cljs-schemas-bundle` at `.github/workflows/test.yml:3874`; checker `implementation/scripts/check-schemas-bundle.cjs`; arms `schemas-bundle-control` / `schemas-bundle-probe` in `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn`, both `:advanced` + `goog.DEBUG=false`, which is what makes the two figures subtractable.
- **Shape:** two-sided gzipped MARGIN between two builds, never an absolute. `MARGIN_MAX_BYTES = 44 * 1024` (`:204`), `MARGIN_MIN_BYTES = 20 * 1024` (`:205`); ceiling = measured margin (39.9 KB) plus ~10% stated headroom; floor catches the probe going vacuous, which is what makes a green mean anything.
- **The non-negotiable design rule this bead adds:** the differential must be chosen so the VOLATILE term cancels. If the quantity you are gating is itself the thing that grows, you have built a ratchet. That is the whole content of Correction 2.
- **Calibrate by making BOTH directions fire before wiring** — per rf2-a9oic, a gate wired without a proven red hands the alerting a false positive on its debut. The exemplar did exactly this (ungating the humanizer: probe 128485 B, margin 41634 B, exit 1; collapsing the probe's require: margin 9.7 KB, exit 1).
- **Measured cost of the exemplar: 47 s cold**, no browser, no Playwright, no Clojure CLI. Any cost figure for a core equivalent is transferred, not measured.
- **Prefer extending an existing job over duplicating JDK + Node + Maven-cache setup and two more builds.** Note that `schemas-bundle-control` ALREADY BUILDS `cljs.core` + `re-frame.core` on every run and reports it (86851 B gzipped at the threshold-setting run) — the core figure is already produced as a byproduct and merely not asserted. Surface-gate on `cljs_prod`. `test.yml` is a one-toucher hot-zone file; sequence against anything else queued for it.

### WHAT rf2-a7ds ALREADY SETTLED — do not re-offer any of it

Closed 2026-09-08. Re-verified at tip:

1. **The nightly bench compile sweep is SHIPPED.** Job `fresco-bench-compile`, "Fresco bench lane compiles (nightly only - rf2-6c12m.1)", `expensive-tests.yml:822`, landed in PR #9533, measured 84 s, running green, and `nightly-result` `needs:` it. **"Add a nightly compile sweep for the benches" is not an option and never will be again.**
2. **Its clause 1 is dead in the tree** — the five arms calling the deleted `rf.fresco/mount!` were migrated in `5c024a0eb3`.
3. **"Reaches no gate" was corrected to "reaches a gate structurally blind to the defect class."** Bench Clojure does arm `lint.yml`'s require-alias-dialect step, but clj-kondo runs there with no classpath and named the deleted var zero times over the pre-fix tree. *An undeclared var is caught by a compiler or by nothing.*
4. **Two inherited operational facts.** The teeth are in `lane_build.cjs` (`:140`), not shadow-cljs, which exits 0 on warnings — any future harness that re-plumbs the build must not bypass it or it inherits a gate that cannot fail. And rf2-6c12m.1 keeps `bench/*` off every per-PR lane by ruling; any proposal putting a bench arm on a PR lane contradicts a standing ruling.

Two gates carrying "perf" in their names measure nothing and should not be mistaken for coverage: `cljs-perf-bundle` and `test:cljs-perf-emit-nightly` are absence-greps, verified at source — neither `check-perf-bundle.cjs` nor `check-bundle-isolation.cjs` asserts a byte threshold. `check-perf-bundle.cjs:50` does usefully reject instrumentation leakage, which overlaps part of what a size budget would buy.

### DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE — refused, by name

- **Any wall-clock RATIO-BAND gate on the browser substrate, PR or nightly.** Refused on the four measurements above. This is the durable ruling.
- **Restoring the 80 MB / 237-file bench run corpus** deleted from main on 2026-08-29 (rf2-6c12m.6, recoverable from `7b492b98cb`). Not restored, and no bench run was performed for this decision. Codex demonstrated the corpus can be read blob-by-blob from git when a specific question needs it — that is the supported access route.
- **Reviving the budget ledger.** `check_budget_ledger.py` is gone from the tree (verified: 0 tracked matches, positive control `check_optional_module_reachability.py` = 1) and has 0 references in `.github/`. `budgets.md` section 7's "never converted into flaky PR thresholds" survives as a **standing ruling worth honouring, not a live gate and not repo-wide law** — it is design history for a closed programme (rf2-6c12m.8).
- **A blanket test backfill or a JVM allocation gate.** The JVM instrument is exact on this box (0.00% spread across 40–60 samples per arm) but is executed nowhere, its runner-portability is unmeasured, and it would grade the JVM/SSR path rather than the browser path a consumer's app runs. Price it only when a specific JVM/SSR workload needs it.
- **A speculative count-assertion sweep.** Codex's suggestion to pin a work-count alongside a behavioural regression is sound but applies only to a CONCRETE named bug. None is named, so there is nothing to dispatch. Existing runtime suites already pin useful work bounds (`index_laws_cljs_test.cljs:314`; `row_total_layer2_dom_cljs_test.cljs:274`, whose browser contrast runs via `test.yml:3514` and is skipped under Node alone).

### THE FOUR UNKNOWNS — kept, unresolved

1. **No historical regression a gate would have caught can be named.** The 2026-07-26 ruling makes "a named regression the gate would have caught" one of three dispatchability conditions, and it is still unmet. This is the single strongest reason the answer is "not now": **there is no demonstrated defect for the proposed gate to prevent.**
2. **The actual gzipped margin for `re-frame.core` has never been measured.** No core bundle-size instrument exists; the ~50 s figure is transferred from the schemas sibling's identical step list.
3. **Whether a JVM allocation gate on `subscribe` is worth building.** Instrument exists (`implementation/core/test/re_frame/bench/read_attribution.clj:66`, `:437`), metric exact on this box, never executed, runner behaviour unknown. If a second axis is ever wanted, this is the one to price — not wall clock.
4. **Whether `budgets.md` section 7 binds anything outside the Fresco programme.** Treated as a standing ruling, not law. See out-of-scope above.

Minor: two bead ids cited by the schemas source (`rf2-n9y35`, `rf2-kybsf`) no longer resolve live; the source and git history substantiate the rulings regardless. Nothing in this ruling depends on a live lookup of either.

*No repo file was edited by this decision. Dossier `ai/decisions/rf2-8o66x.performance-regression-gate.md` retired after this note verified.*

== NAME CORRECTION, 2026-09-10 (rf2-j8lg) ==

This bead's DESCRIPTION and NOTES carried the RETIRED PRODUCT NAME. The tree was renamed by PR #9568
(rf2-d1nr.2, 2026-09-09); the tracker was not, because `scripts/check_retired_spellings.py`
grades tracked SOURCE and does not read bead prose. The substitution was mechanical in all three
case forms and asserted NAME-ONLY line by line — both sides normalised by blanking either name,
"lines changed by anything else: 0" — and every replacement target was verified live in the tree
before the write.

Nothing needed rewording: every occurrence was a plain USE of the product name — a path, a
coordinate, a keyword or the name itself — rather than prose DESCRIBING the rename, which a
blanket replace would have turned into "rename B to B".

CLOSED beads were left untouched: a closed bead records what was true when it was written.

MAYOR BACKLOG REREAD 2026-08-16 15:55 AUSEST — THE TITLE'S PREMISE HAS INVERTED, THE HOLD HAS NOT. Recording both because this is the dangerous combination: a future reader who verifies the TITLE will find it false and conclude the bead is dispatchable, when the actual ruling rests on something else entirely and still stands.

TITLE PREMISE, NOW FALSE: 'every bench in the repo covers an UNPUBLISHED artefact'. Measured at tip 3d04311b2c — implementation/hicasso/deps.edn carries clein build config (6 mentions, identical in shape to tools/xray/deps.edn which is a known-published coordinate), and CHANGELOG.md names day8/re-frame2-hicasso as published under rf2-gra70. So the hicasso bench lane now covers a PUBLISHED artefact, which is exactly what the title says nothing in the repo does. The retire also removed the seventeen Freehand B-spine arms that were the clearest instance of the original complaint.

THE RULING'S REASON IS THE NOISE FLOOR AND IT IS UNTOUCHED. The 2026-07-26 mayor ruling defers on a MEASURED ground, not a preference: the no-substrate floor arm drifted 37% across rounds — larger than most of the effects being measured — and the same primitive read 10.4ns and 21.7ns across two JVMs on one box. A regression gate on a substrate with a 37% floor drift is a flake generator, and this repo's standing rule that a failing test on a touched surface is NEVER a flake is precisely what makes a false red expensive. rf2-yumaq is the worked example: G-8 died because its baseline was too fast.

NOTHING IN THIS SESSION BEARS ON THAT NUMBER. The measurement lane has been building instruments all day, but no window has been taken since the fleet has not been idle, so the floor drift is neither confirmed nor refuted at tip.

SO: STAY DEFERRED, and the release condition is a measured floor rather than a date. Whoever revisits should re-take the floor drift first — if the lane's new instruments bring it under control, the ruling's own reasoning releases the bead. The evidence it cites still resolves: docs/design/freehand/studio/compiled-tier-browser-worth-it.md survives the retire (docs/design/freehand/ is deliberately kept, 37 tracked files).

RETITLE WHEN SOMEONE TOUCHES IT NEXT — the current title will mislead again.

title: Skill review: skills/re-frame2-implementor - completeness, correctness, organisation, skill best practice
description:
Review the `re-frame2-implementor` skill: skills/re-frame2-implementor/, meaning SKILL.md and every reference and script under it. Do it in four SERIAL passes, finishing each one, and fixing what it finds, before starting the next:

1. COMPLETENESS. Does the skill cover what its description promises, and what an agent invoking it will need? Look for gaps against the current spec/ and implementation/: features, APIs, workflows and failure modes this skill's audience will meet. Also look for references the SKILL.md points at that are missing or empty.
2. CORRECTNESS. Check every claim against spec/ and implementation/ at trunk: API names, signatures, keywords, reserved namespaces, file paths, commands and code examples. Look for names that no longer exist, behaviour that has changed, dead links, and examples that would not compile or run as written.
3. ORGANISATION AND STRUCTURE. SKILL.md should be a concise entry point. References should be split by topic, sit one level deep, and be linked directly from SKILL.md. Nothing should be duplicated across files, terminology should be consistent, and a reader should find what they need in the order they need it.
4. SKILL BEST PRACTICE (Anthropic's Agent Skills authoring guidance).
   - Frontmatter: `name`, and a `description` in the third person that says what the skill does AND when to use it, with specific trigger terms.
   - A lean SKILL.md body (well under ~500 lines) that uses progressive disclosure into reference files.
   - No time-sensitive or history narrative.
   - Concrete examples, and checklists for workflows where order matters.
   - Scripts for deterministic operations rather than prose instructions.

DELIVERABLE: one PR applying the fixes, whose body summarises what each pass found and changed. Report findings outside skills/re-frame2-implementor/ (spec/, implementation/, skills/README.md, another skill) rather than editing them. skills/README.md is shared by every skill, so name any change it needs and do not make it.

POSTURE: fix real defects and improve structure where that pays a reader. Do not rewrite for style. Present-tense convention: no bead ids and no history in the skill text.

GATES: `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` (skills/ is a docs-gate root), and the api-manifest skills check, `clojure -M -m re-frame.api-manifest.skills-check` from implementation/scripts/api-manifest (lint.yml's api-manifest job), which fails on a non-manifest API reference. Run `scripts/check_readme_inventories.py` if an inventory is touched. CI covers the rest.

title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: implementation/scripts (Node suite and api-manifest)
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: implementation/scripts (Node suite and api-manifest). This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.16 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.16 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.16 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.16) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/scripts (Node suite and api-manifest). Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/scripts (Node suite and api-manifest). Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/scripts (Node suite and api-manifest) to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/scripts (Node suite and api-manifest); a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/scripts (Node suite and api-manifest) plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/scripts (Node suite and api-manifest) that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: resources: a cross-frame reply whose work-id collides with the receiving frame's live work-id clears the receiving frame's ledger row (suspected, unreproduced)
description:
Found by the rf2-nvxtm.19 worker (resources pruning, PR #11205) by reading the code, NOT reproduced. Re-derive every site at tip.

A cross-frame reply whose work-id collides with a work-id already live in the RECEIVING frame takes the stale branch. That settles and clears the receiving frame's own ledger row and handle, which contradicts the `live-slot-for-reply` docstring. Sites: implementation/resources mutation_events.cljc around :1903 and :2308, and events.cljc around :2588 and :2809. No test covers the case.

TASK: reproduce first with a JVM test (a reply from frame A whose work-id equals an in-flight work-id in frame B, delivered to B). If it reproduces, fix it so a reply resolves only against its own frame's slot, as the docstring promises, and keep the test as the regression guard (red before, green after). If it does not reproduce, record the evidence and close with that. Exact fix only; no redesign of the ledger.
Gates: the resources JVM lane (clojure -M:test from implementation/resources), counts before and after; clj-kondo on touched source, run without --fail-level. If the fix touches a .cljc branch that only CLJS compiles, say so, and rely on CI's :node-test.

== WORKER RESULT (fix-xframe-reply, 2026-10-14 AUSEST) — REPRODUCED AND FIXED, PR #11208

REPRODUCED. A JVM test (new file implementation/resources/test/re_frame/resources_cross_frame_reply_ledger_cljs_test.cljc) has frames A and B issue the same work on one recorded allocation ({:generation 1 :counter 1}), so both hold the same work-id. It then delivers A's reply into B. Against the unfixed code all six cases were red (3 tests, 18 assertions, 6 failures, exit 1): resource, infinite-feed page and mutation replies, each on success and failure. In every case B's ledger row went :running -> :suppressed {:reason :stale-reply ...} and B's host handle went to nil. B's slot stayed :loading / :pending with :current-work pointing at the now-terminal row. The fixture assertions and the control assertions (the same reply into A settles A) passed.

CAUSE. live-slot-for-reply rejects a reply stamped for another frame. But the rejected reply falls into the handler's stale branch, and all six stale branches (events.cljc succeeded / failed / page-succeeded / page-failed; mutation_events.cljc succeeded / failed) ran clear-handle! plus settle-terminal :suppressed under that work-id in the RECEIVING frame.

FIX. New reply-handlers/settle-suppressed-work! owns that clear-handle + settle-terminal pair. For a cross-frame reply (stamped :rf.frame/id non-nil and not the receiving frame) it settles nothing and returns {}. live-slot-for-reply uses the same cross-frame-reply? predicate. Same-frame stale suppression is unchanged, and the stale-suppressed trace still fires. No #?(:cljs) production branch touched.

   runner actually executes each file in tools/mcp-base; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.

   refer to.

title: Spec 005 §Lessons from xstate states the superseded 'XState is the parity reference; align unless substrate-constrained' rule; restate the ruled statecharts posture
description:
Spec 005 states a superseded posture for machines. Restate it to match Mike's 2026-10-15 ruling, which is recorded as the close reason of the decision bead this one is discovered from.

## The ruling, in short

re-frame2 machines aim at an excellent statecharts implementation that is re-frame and ClojureScript native. XState is admired as the state of the art, and its features are ones we aspire to support, expressed the re-frame way. XState is a reference, not a parity target.

  - the goal is an excellent statecharts implementation, native to re-frame and ClojureScript;
  - XState (v6 direction) is the admired reference whose features re-frame2 aims to support, expressed natively (topology as data, keywords and registered ids, pure callbacks returning `{:data :fx}`, the per-frame router, managed effects and subscriptions);

title: A registered Form-2 view emits render evidence for its outer construction call only, so its re-renders are invisible to Xray and Story
description:
A registered Form-2 view emits its render evidence for the outer construction call only. Every later render runs outside the per-render scope, so tracing never sees it.

## Where

`build-frame-aware-view` in `implementation/core/src/re_frame/views.cljs` sets up the per-render scope around `(apply render args)`:
- the `*render-key*` / `*view-deref-sink*` bindings and `with-handler-scope`;
- `:rf.view/render`;
- the `rf.performance/mark-and-measure :render` bracket;
- `emit-view-rendered-trace!` (`:rf.view/rendered`).

When that call returns a Form-2 inner fn, `implementation/core/src/re_frame/views/source_coord_annotation.cljs` only annotates it: `(fn form-2-wrapper [& args] (inject-source-coord-attr id coord-attr (apply out args)))` (~L166). When the debug or wrap gate is off, `out` is returned bare. Reagent and reagent-slim store that inner fn and call it directly on every later render, outside all of the bindings above.

## Consequences

- A `subscribe` inside the inner body never reaches `:deref-subs`.
- Later renders emit no `:rf.view/rendered`, although Spec 009's trace table promises one event per reactive view re-rendered, and `views.cljs` says it "fires on every render".
- `:elapsed-ms` and the `rf:render:<id>` measure time only the outer call.
- `:sub/run` sees a nil render-key.

Xray's Reactive and Views panels, and Story's `:rf.assert/caused` / `:rf.assert/no-cascade-rerender`, read these rows. To all of them a Form-2 view appears to render once.

## Change

When the render returns a plain fn (not `reagent-class?`), treat the outer call as construction and emit nothing for it. Return an inner wrapper that runs the same per-render scope on every call, with `:mount? true` on the first inner call and annotation when enabled.

Preserve:
- the outer body runs exactly once per mount;
- macro-injected `dispatch`/`subscribe` are captured once;
- Form-3 class pass-through and the direct-class `apply` path;
- no wrapper element is added;
- production elision.

Do NOT add raw-Reaction deref tracking, and do not rewrite the renderer. The deref sink records at `subscribe`, and that stays.

## Sequencing

`source_coord_annotation.cljs` is also edited by the bead that deletes the non-DOM-root warning (it depends on this one). Land this one first.

The gate is `npm run test:cljs` and/or the browser lane, which needs a shadow-cljs lane grant. The change is CLJS-only.

Two reviews found this independently (Opus adapters action 8 and core-reactive-substrate action 3; Sol 17 §2). 2. The outer factory body runs once per mount, and injected `dispatch`/`subscribe` are captured once.
3. Form-1 and Form-3 emission counts are unchanged. The existing Form-2 annotation and prod-elision tests stay green on stock Reagent and reagent-slim.
